name: Air Cycle Machine (ACM)
function: Bootstrap air-refrigeration unit consisting of a centrifugal compressor, expansion turbine, and ram-air cooling fan mounted on a single common shaft supported by air bearings. Cools high-pressure, high-temperature bleed air by extracting mechanical work across the expansion turbine, producing sub-zero air for the air conditioning pack.
location: Unpressurized under-wing belly fairing (Air Conditioning Pack Bay)
simple: Think of the ACM as a refrigerator that runs on compressed air instead of chemical Freon. It takes blistering +200°C air bled off the jet engines, spins it through a turbine at tens of thousands of RPM to shed heat energy, and chills it to freezing temperatures in a split second so the passenger cabin stays cool.

name: Outflow Valve (OFV)
function: Electrically actuated modulating butterfly or flapper door that regulates cabin pressurization by varying the rate at which conditioned cabin air is exhausted overboard. Driven by automatic electric motors (controlled by the Cabin Pressure Controllers) and a manual backup motor to maintain the desired cabin altitude and differential pressure.
location: Aft lower fuselage skin, below the flotation waterline
simple: An airplane cabin is inflated like a leaky balloon: the air-conditioning packs constantly pump fresh air IN, and this motorized trapdoor near the tail pinches open or closed by millimeters to control how fast air leaks OUT—keeping your ears comfortable at 38,000 feet.

name: Flight Management Guidance Computer (FMGC / FMC)
function: Core dual-redundant autoflight computer performing flight management (lateral/vertical navigation, performance optimization, fuel prediction, and radio autotuning) and flight guidance (autopilot, flight director, and autothrust/autothrottle command laws) from takeoff to autoland.
location: Forward Avionics Bay (E&E Bay)
simple: The navigational and autopilot brain of the cockpit. One half calculates the most fuel-efficient 4D route and speeds from takeoff to touchdown, while the other half steers the flight controls and throttles to follow that path automatically.

name: Flight Control Unit (FCU) / Mode Control Panel (MCP)
function: Primary tactical cockpit interface for the autoflight system. Houses rotary selector knobs for Airspeed/Mach, Heading/Track, Altitude, and Vertical Speed/Flight Path Angle, plus engagement pushbuttons for Autopilot, Autothrottle/Autothrust, Approach, and Flight Director modes.
location: Cockpit Center Glareshield Panel
simple: Mounted right below the front windshield within easy reach of both pilots, this is the dashboard control bar for the autopilot where pilots dial in assigned altitudes, headings, and airspeeds given by Air Traffic Control.

name: VHF Communication Transceiver
function: Provides line-of-sight amplitude-modulated voice and digital VDL Mode 2 data communications (ACARS) across the aviation VHF band (118.000–136.992 MHz with 8.33 kHz or 25 kHz channel spacing). Typically three transceivers are installed for primary ATC voice, secondary monitoring, and digital data link.
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack
simple: The primary two-way radio box that lets pilots talk to Air Traffic Control towers and radar centers—while also beaming digital text messages (ACARS) between the aircraft and airline operations on the ground.

name: Generator Control Unit (GCU)
function: Solid-state controller that monitors and regulates the excitation field of each AC generator to hold output at a steady 115/200V 400 Hz. Protects the electrical network by automatically tripping the Generator Line Contactor on overvoltage, undervoltage, under/overfrequency, or differential short-circuit faults.
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack
simple: The electronic brain and circuit-protector watching over each electrical generator. It keeps voltage rock-steady at 115 volts and instantly disconnects the generator in milliseconds if it detects a short circuit or dangerous power surge.

name: Transformer Rectifier Unit (TRU)
function: Steps down three-phase 115/200V 400 Hz AC power using a step-down transformer and converts it via a full-wave silicon rectifier into 28V DC power for DC buses, avionics, relays, and battery charging.
location: Forward Avionics Bay / Electrical distribution bay
simple: Just like the power brick on a laptop cord converts high-voltage wall AC into low-voltage DC, the TRU converts the airplane's heavy 115V AC generator power into 28V DC power for cockpit computers, valves, and lights.

name: Fire Detection Unit (FDU)
function: Dual-channel electronic evaluator that continuously monitors resistance and pneumatic pressure/capacitance signals from Loop A and Loop B fire and overheat sensing elements in the engines and APU compartment. Uses AND logic between both loops to trigger cockpit fire bells and master warning lights.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: Constantly listens to two separate heat-sensing wire loops wrapped around each engine and the APU. If both loops report extreme heat at the same time, the FDU rings the loud red fire bell in the cockpit.

name: Elevator Aileron Computer (ELAC) / Primary Flight Computer
function: Primary digital fly-by-wire flight control computer commanding normal pitch (elevators and horizontal stabilizer) and roll (ailerons). Computes flight envelope protections including load-factor limitation (+2.5G to -1.0G), pitch attitude protection, high-angle-of-attack stall protection, and high-speed protection.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: On a fly-by-wire airliner, moving the cockpit control stick sends an electrical signal to this computer, which calculates the exact elevator and aileron angles needed for a smooth ride while refusing to let the airplane stall or overstress its wings.

name: Slat Flap Control Computer (SFCC) / Flap Slat Electronics Unit
function: Dual-channel computer that controls and monitors leading-edge slats and trailing-edge flaps. Translates cockpit flap lever positions into hydraulic Power Control Unit commands, prevents slat retraction at high angles of attack, and engages wingtip brakes if asymmetry, skew, or overspeed is detected.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: Controls the high-lift slats and flaps on the wings during takeoff and landing. If it ever senses that the left flap is extending faster or further than the right flap, it slams hydraulic brakes shut in milliseconds so the airplane doesn't roll uncontrollably.

name: Aileron Hydraulic Servocontrol (PCU)
function: Electro-hydraulic servoactuator that converts electrical flight-control commands into 3,000 psi hydraulic force to deflect the left and right ailerons. Each aileron is driven by two servocontrols connected to independent hydraulic systems, operating in active/damping pairs.
location: Outboard wing rear spar / aileron hinge shroud box
simple: The hydraulic muscle inside the wing that physically pushes the ailerons up and down to bank the airplane left and right. Each aileron has two actuators: one actively pushes while the second rides along as a shock damper and instant backup.

name: Fuel Tank Boost Pump
function: Three-phase 115V 400 Hz AC centrifugal pump mounted inside a self-sealing canister housing at the bottom of the wing and center fuel tanks. Supplies fuel under positive pressure (~25–45 psi) to the engine low-pressure fuel manifold, preventing vapor lock and cavitation at high altitude.
location: Wing and center tank sumps, accessible via lower wing skin panels
simple: Electric pumps sitting at the bottom of the fuel tanks that push kerosene forward to the engines under positive pressure. Their housing includes a one-way check valve canister so a mechanic can swap a broken pump cartridge from under the wing without draining a full tank of fuel!

name: Fuel Quantity Capacitance Probe (FQI)
function: Concentric tubular capacitance sensor immersed vertically inside the wing and center fuel tanks. Measures electrical capacitance changes between Jet A-1 fuel (dielectric constant ~2.1) and air (~1.0), enabling the Fuel Quantity Computer to calculate exact fuel mass regardless of aircraft pitch/roll attitude or thermal expansion.
location: Distributed inside inner, outer, and center wing fuel tanks
simple: A car fuel gauge uses a simple floating ball that gets fooled whenever you drive uphill. An airliner uses dozens of vertical metal tubes inside the wing that measure electrical capacitance through the kerosene—calculating the exact weight of fuel in kilograms even when the wings flex or the nose pitches up.

name: Engine-Driven Hydraulic Pump (EDP)
function: Variable-displacement inline axial-piston pump bolted to each engine's accessory gearbox. Automatically varies its internal swashplate angle to maintain a constant 3,000 psi (or 5,000 psi on newest widebodies) system pressure across varying flow demands.
location: Left and Right Engine Accessory Gearboxes
simple: The heavy-duty mechanical pump bolted directly to each jet engine's gearbox. Whenever the engine is spinning, this pump squeezes purple Skydrol hydraulic fluid up to 3,000 PSI to power the landing gear, wheel brakes, and wing flight controls.

name: Hydraulic Power Transfer Unit (PTU)
function: Reversible or unidirectional mechanically coupled hydraulic motor-pump assembly linking two independent hydraulic systems. Activates automatically when differential pressure exceeds a preset threshold (e.g., 500 psi), using fluid pressure from the healthy system to spin a pump on the depressurized system without mixing a single drop of fluid between reservoirs.
location: Main Landing Gear Wheel Well / Belly Hydraulic Bay
simple: Famous on Airbus jets for making the rhythmic 'barking dog' sound under the cabin floor during engine start! If one engine is shut down, the PTU uses hydraulic pressure from the running side to spin a pump on the dead side—keeping both hydraulic systems pressurized without ever mixing their fluids.

name: Probe Heat Computer (PHC)
function: Solid-state controller managing electrical anti-ice heating for the Captain's, First Officer's, and Standby pitot probes, static ports, Angle-of-Attack (AoA) vanes, and Total Air Temperature (TAT) sensors. Automatically switches pitot heating from reduced power on the ground to full wattage in flight.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: Controls the high-wattage electric heaters inside the external nose sensors so supercooled cloud ice can never freeze over the airspeed or stall vanes. On the ground, it throttles heat down so the probes don't burn out without wind cooling.

name: Flight Warning Computer (FWC)
function: Dual-redundant avionics unit that monitors aircraft system buses across all flight phases to generate red Master Warning / amber Master Caution lights, ECAM/EICAS text checklists, continuous repetitive chimes, and synthetic voice radio-altitude callouts. Inhibits non-critical cautions during high-workload takeoff and landing phases.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: The cockpit's intelligent alarm manager. It knows whether the plane is in the middle of a critical 130-knot takeoff roll or cruising calmly at 36,000 feet—holding back minor caution chimes during takeoff so pilots aren't distracted, and displaying step-by-step checklists on the center screen.

name: Cockpit Electronic Display Unit (DU)
function: Interchangeable high-brightness Active-Matrix LCD screen presenting Primary Flight Display (PFD), Navigation Display (ND), Engine/Warning Display (E/WD or EICAS), and System Display (SD) symbology generated by the Display Management Computers.
location: Cockpit Main Instrument Panel
simple: The six square glass screens in the cockpit. Because all six screens are identical interchangeable hardware boxes, if the Captain's primary flight screen ever fails, the computer automatically shifts the flight instruments onto the neighboring screen!

name: Landing Gear Control and Interface Unit (LGCIU) / PSEU
function: Dual-redundant proximity-sensing and sequencing computer that controls the hydraulic sequence of opening gear doors, retracting/extending the landing gear legs, and latching uplocks. Also broadcasts vital 'Weight-on-Wheels' (Air/Ground mode) signals to pressurization, flight control, and thrust reverser computers.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: Choreographs the mechanical ballet of raising and lowering the landing gear so the heavy wheels never slam into closed gear doors—and tells every other computer on the airplane the exact split-second the wheels leave or touch the runway.

image.alt: Landing Gear Control and Interface Unit (LGCIU)

name: Braking and Steering Control Unit (BSCU) / Antiskid Computer
function: Dual-channel digital computer governing normal hydraulic wheel braking, anti-skid modulation (comparing individual wheel tachometers against aircraft reference speed), autobrake deceleration rates, and electro-hydraulic Nose Wheel Steering from cockpit tillers and rudder pedals.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: Works like your car's ABS computer and power-steering module combined on steroids: it stops the tyres from skidding and bursting on wet runways, applies smooth automatic braking on touchdown, and steers the nosewheel on the taxiway.

name: Main Landing Gear Carbon Multi-Disc Brake Assembly
function: Multi-disc Reinforced Carbon-Carbon (RCC) friction brake pack consisting of alternating rotating rotors (keyed to the wheel rim) and stationary stators (keyed to the axle) squeezed by a ring of hydraulic pistons. Absorbs extreme kinetic energy during landing or Rejected Takeoff past 1,200°C without melting.
location: Main Landing Gear wheel axles
simple: Instead of steel brake pads that would melt and weld together during a 160-knot emergency stop, airliners use a clutch-pack of pure Carbon-Carbon discs inside each main wheel that can glow bright orange past 1,000°C and actually get stronger as they heat up.

name: Air Data Inertial Reference Unit (ADIRU)
function: Triple-redundant navigation core combining an Air Data Reference (ADR) module (computing barometric altitude, IAS, TAS, Mach, TAT, and AoA from pitot/static inputs) and a Ring-Laser Gyro Inertial Reference (IR) module (computing autonomous attitude, pitch, roll, true/magnetic heading, groundspeed, and present position).
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack
simple: Even if every GPS satellite and ground radio station on Earth shut off, the three ADIRUs allow an airliner to navigate across oceans using spinning laser beams (Ring Laser Gyros) and accelerometers that feel every millimeter of movement, paired with outside air-pressure data.

name: Pitot Probe (Total Pressure Sensor)
function: Electrically anti-iced L-shaped stagnation pressure tube facing directly into the undisturbed relative airflow. Captures Total Pressure (Pt) and routes it to an Air Data Module or Air Data Computer where Static Pressure (Ps) is subtracted to calculate Indicated Airspeed (IAS) and Mach number.
location: Forward fuselage nose exterior skin below cockpit windows (Captain, F/O, and Standby)
simple: Three small heated metal tubes sticking out of the nose like shark fins. By measuring how hard oncoming air molecules slam into the front hole of the tube, the aircraft calculates its true flying speed through the air.

name: Angle of Attack (AoA) Sensor Vane
function: Electrically heated, counterweighted aerodynamic weathervane or slotted probe protruding through the forward fuselage skin. Aligns continuously with local airflow to measure the exact angle between the wing chord and oncoming air, feeding the air data and flight control computers for Stall Warning and Stick Shaker/Alpha Protection.
location: Forward fuselage exterior skin, both sides of the nose
simple: Three small pivoting metal fins on the outside of the nose that act like high-speed weathervanes. They tell the flight computers the exact upward angle the wing is slicing through the air so the airplane knows immediately if it is getting close to an aerodynamic stall.

name: TCAS II Computer (Traffic Alert & Collision Avoidance)
function: Airborne collision avoidance processor connected to top and bottom directional antennas. Interrogates Mode C and Mode S transponders of surrounding aircraft on 1030/1090 MHz, calculates time-to-closest-approach (Tau), and generates visual/vocal Traffic Advisories (TAs) and coordinated vertical Resolution Advisories (RAs).
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack
simple: An independent plane-to-plane radar guardian that talks directly to the transponders of every nearby aircraft once per second. If two airplanes ever get on a collision course, their TCAS computers negotiate in milliseconds and shout 'CLIMB!' to one cockpit and 'DESCEND!' to the other.

name: Air Conditioning System / Pack Controller (ACSC / ZC)
function: Dual-channel digital controller that regulates Pack 1 and Pack 2 discharge temperatures, Pack Flow Control Valves, bypass valves, ram-air inlet/outlet flaps, and cabin zone trim-air valves to maintain Cockpit, Forward Cabin, and Aft Cabin temperatures at pilot-selected targets.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: The smart thermostat computer for the entire aircraft. It blends freezing air from the belly air-conditioning packs with a trickle of hot engine bleed air ('trim air') so the cockpit, front cabin, and back cabin can each stay at their own custom temperature.

name: Avionics Equipment Ventilation Controller (AEVC)
function: Controls and monitors cooling airflow through the cockpit instrument panels, circuit breaker panels, and under-floor E&E avionics racks. Commands the blower fan, extract fan, and skin heat-exchanger inlet/outlet valves between Open-Circuit (ground warm weather), Closed-Circuit (in-flight/cold weather), and Smoke configuration.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: Dozens of cockpit computers generate as much heat as a room full of gaming PCs. This controller opens external belly vents on hot tarmac days to blow fresh air across the computer racks, then seals the vents in flight and circulates the air through cold fuselage skin ducts.

name: Cabin Pressure Controller (CPC)
function: Dual digital pressurization computers that receive cruise flight level and landing field elevation data from the Flight Management System and air data computers to compute the optimal cabin altitude schedule. Alternates active control between System 1 and System 2 on each flight to drive the Outflow Valve motors.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: Calculates how fast the cabin pressure should climb and descend so your ears barely feel a pop—making sure cabin pressure smoothly matches the arrival airport's elevation right as the wheels touch the runway.

name: Pack Flow Control & Shutoff Valve (FCV)
function: Pneumatically operated, electrically controlled butterfly shutoff and flow-regulating valve mounted upstream of each Air Conditioning Pack. Regulates hot bleed-air mass flow (LO, NORM, HI) entering the pack and automatically closes during main engine starting or when an engine fire switch is pulled.
location: Under-wing Belly Pack Bay inlet duct
simple: The main gatekeeper valve at the entrance to each air-conditioning pack. It adjusts how much air flows into the cabin based on passenger load and automatically slams shut for 45 seconds during pushback so all air pressure goes to start the main engines.

name: Cabin Air Recirculation Fan & HEPA Filter
function: High-efficiency axial vane fan that draws ~40–50% of spent cabin air through hospital-grade HEPA (High-Efficiency Particulate Air) microbial filters and routes it into the Mixing Manifold to blend with 50% fresh conditioned pack air—reducing engine bleed-air extraction and saving cruise fuel burn.
location: Under-floor air conditioning mixing bay
simple: Draws cabin air through 99.97% HEPA filters (the same grade used in surgical operating rooms) and mixes it 50/50 with fresh outside air from the packs every 2 to 3 minutes, keeping cabin air clean while reducing fuel burn.

name: Cabin Positive & Negative Pressure Safety Relief Valve
function: Two independent spring-loaded pneumatic poppet valves mounted in the aft pressure bulkhead. Require zero electrical power to operate: they crack open outward at ~8.6 psi differential pressure to prevent structural fuselage over-pressurization, or open inward at -0.5 to -1.0 psi to prevent vacuum crushing during a rapid descent.
location: Aft Rear Pressure Bulkhead
simple: Even if every pressurization computer and outflow valve jammed shut at the same time, these two purely mechanical spring-loaded relief valves in the back wall of the cabin pop open automatically to stop the fuselage from over-inflating.

name: Residual Pressure Control Unit (RPCU)
function: Autonomous safety controller that monitors landing gear squat switches and engine speed on the ground. Automatically drives the Outflow Valve full open if the aircraft is parked on the ground and both Cabin Pressure Controllers fail to depressurize the hull, preventing violent door-opening accidents.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: A backup safety guardian that forces the outflow valve wide open after landing so even 0.5 PSI of trapped air pressure can never remain inside the cabin when ground crew or flight attendants unlatch a cabin door.

name: Catalytic Ozone Converter
function: Honeycomb catalytic core canister installed in the hot bleed-air supply duct upstream of the Air Conditioning Packs. Uses a precious-metal palladium/manganese catalyst to dissociate toxic stratospheric tri-atomic ozone ($O_3$) molecules into harmless breathable di-atomic oxygen ($O_2$) before the air enters the cabin.
location: Belly Air Conditioning Pack Bay inlet ducting
simple: Up at 38,000 feet, outside air contains natural ozone gas that causes headaches, coughing, and eye irritation if breathed indoors. This catalytic converter breaks stratospheric ozone ($O_3$) down into normal breathable oxygen ($O_2$) before it enters the cabin.

name: Trim Air Pressure Regulating Valve (TAPRV) & Zone Trim Valves
function: Pneumatic pressure regulator and stepper-motor Zone Trim Air Valves that tap hot bleed air downstream of the pack flow valve, regulate it to ~4 psi above cabin pressure, and meter precise amounts of warm air into individual cabin zones (Cockpit, Forward Cabin, Aft Cabin).
location: Under-floor air conditioning mixing bay
simple: Instead of running giant air-conditioning packs at different temperatures for each part of the plane, the packs cool all air down to the coldest zone's need, and these Trim Air Valves add a precise trickle of hot air back into the zones that want to be warmer.

name: Pack Ram Air Door & Emergency Ram Air Inlet Actuator
function: Linear electromechanical actuators driving the Pack Ram Air Inlet/Outlet doors (modulating cooling airflow across the primary and main heat exchangers) and the Emergency Ram Air Inlet valve, which opens below 10,000 ft unpressurized to ventilate the cabin with outside ram air if both packs fail or smoke must be cleared.
location: Belly fairing unpressurized pack bay
simple: Scoops outside wind into the belly radiators to cool the packs—and if both air conditioning packs ever fail or the cabin fills with smoke at low altitude, opening the Emergency Ram Air door scoops fresh outside air straight into the cabin ducts.

name: Lavatory & Galley Vent Extraction Fan
function: Continuously running electric centrifugal exhaust fan that draws air from all cabin lavatories and galley ceiling hoods and discharges it overboard near the Outflow Valve—keeping lavatory odors and galley oven heat from migrating into the passenger seating zones.
location: Aft under-floor fuselage near outflow valve
simple: Pulls air continuously out of every bathroom ceiling vent and kitchen galley so food smells, oven heat, and bathroom odors are sucked straight out of the back of the airplane instead of drifting into the passenger seats.

name: Cargo Compartment Heating & Ventilation Controller
function: Conditioned Service Air System controller, trim valve, and isolation valves that regulate temperature and ventilation inside the pressurized belly cargo compartments so live animals, pharmaceuticals, and perishable freight do not freeze at cruise altitude. Automatically seals shut upon cargo smoke detection.
location: Forward Avionics Bay and Belly Cargo Bulkheads
simple: Keeps the pressurized baggage holds under the floor ventilated and heated so pets, tropical flowers, and temperature-sensitive medicines stay safe at 38,000 feet—and automatically seals the vents shut if a cargo smoke detector trips.

name: Primary & Main Ram Air Heat Exchangers
function: Dual air-to-air aluminum plate-fin radiators inside each Air Conditioning Pack. The Primary Heat Exchanger cools incoming engine bleed air before it enters the ACM compressor; the Main Heat Exchanger cools the re-compressed air using outside ram air before it expands across the ACM cold turbine.
location: Left and Right Belly Air Conditioning Pack Bays
simple: Two heavy-duty aluminum radiators inside each belly pack that use freezing outside wind ('ram air') to strip the first wave of heat out of the +200°C engine air before the Air Cycle Machine chills it down to zero.

name: Pack Reheater, Condenser & High-Pressure Water Extractor
function: Closed-loop dehumidification assembly inside the Air Conditioning Pack. Cools humid compressed air until water vapor condenses into droplets, spins the droplets out via centrifugal vanes inside the Water Extractor, and sprays that water onto the ram-air heat exchanger while preventing ice from clogging the ACM turbine.
location: Belly Air Conditioning Pack Bays 1 and 2
simple: On a muggy monsoon day, pumping humid air straight into a sub-zero air conditioning turbine would blow snow and fog out of the cabin vents! This water separator wrings gallons of liquid water out of the air before it reaches the cabin.

name: Low-Pressure (LP) Pre-Conditioned Ground Air Inlet
function: 8-inch diameter belly receptacle fitted with a spring-loaded non-return check valve that connects directly to the cabin Mixing Unit. Allows an airport gate Pre-Conditioned Air (PCA) hose to pump chilled or heated air directly into the cabin ducts without running the aircraft's APU or Packs.
location: Forward lower fuselage belly fairing
simple: That big wide yellow or insulated hose you see snaking from the boarding bridge to the belly of the parked plane at the gate—pumping cold air-conditioned air straight into the cabin so the airline can leave the fuel-burning APU switched off.

name: Flight Augmentation Computer (FAC) / Yaw Damper Computer
function: Dual-redundant flight control and envelope computer that controls electrically driven Rudder Trim, Yaw Damper servoactuators, and Rudder Travel Limitation. Also computes characteristic speed tape markers (minimum selectable speed VLS, stall/alpha protection speeds, Green Dot best lift-to-drag speed) and reactive windshear detection.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: Manages the rudder on the tail (stopping the tail from fishtailing in turbulence and limiting rudder travel at high speed so the tailfin can never be overstressed), while also calculating the safe-speed bars displayed on the pilots' speed tape.

name: Multipurpose Control and Display Unit (MCDU / CDU)
function: Full alphanumeric keyboard and color LCD scratchpad interface located on the center pedestal. Used by pilots to program flight plans, airway waypoints, takeoff speeds (V1, VR, V2), and weight/CG into the Flight Management Computers, and used by maintenance engineers to run BITE diagnostic tests.
location: Cockpit Center Pedestal forward console
simple: The twin keyboard-and-screen units on the center console between the pilots. Pilots type their flight plan, fuel weight, and takeoff speeds into the MCDU before departure, and mechanics use the exact same screen to read computer fault codes at the gate.

name: Rudder Trim Selector Switch & Digital Position Indicator
function: Spring-loaded rotary NOSE LEFT / NOSE RIGHT switch and center RESET pushbutton paired with a digital LED Rudder Trim position display on the center pedestal. Sends manual trim requests to the Flight Augmentation / Yaw Damper computers when the autopilot is disengaged.
location: Cockpit Center Pedestal aft panel
simple: Allows the pilots to trim the tail rudder up to 20 degrees left or right—essential if one engine fails in flight and the remaining working engine is pushing the airplane sideways.

name: Radio Management Panel (RMP)
function: Dual microprocessor control panel with active/standby LED frequency windows, transfer key, and dual concentric tuning knobs. Tunes all VHF and HF communication radios, and includes a guarded backup navigation mode allowing pilots to manually tune VOR, ILS, and ADF receivers if both Flight Management Computers fail.
location: Cockpit Center Pedestal
simple: The cockpit radio tuner where pilots dial in the next Air Traffic Control frequency into the 'Standby' window and press the transfer arrow to make it 'Active' with a single click.

name: Audio Control Panel (ACP) & Audio Management Unit (AMU)
function: Three cockpit Audio Control Panels (Captain, First Officer, Third Occupant) wired to a central Audio Management Unit in the avionics bay. Routes headset, boom mic, oxygen-mask mic, hand mic, and cockpit loudspeaker audio across VHF, HF, SATCOM, cabin PA, ground mechanic interphone, and navigation Morse identifiers.
location: Cockpit Center Pedestal / Overhead Panel and Forward Avionics Bay
simple: The audio mixing board in the cockpit that lets the Captain talk to Air Traffic Control on VHF 1 while the First Officer listens to the weather broadcast on VHF 2 or talks to the ground mechanic on the nose headset without talking over each other.

name: Cabin Intercommunication Data System (CIDS) / Cabin Management Computer
function: Dual central cabin computers (Active and Hot-Standby) networked to overhead Decoder/Encoder Units (DEUs) along the cabin ceiling. Controls passenger reading lights, 'Fasten Seatbelt' / 'Return to Seat' signs, cabin chimes, PA announcements, flight attendant call lights, lavatory smoke indicators, and escape-slide pressure alerts.
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack
simple: Every single reading light, 'Fasten Seatbelt' chime, flight-attendant call button, and PA speaker inside the passenger cabin is controlled by this central computer.

name: Forward Attendant Panel (FAP) & Prerecorded Announcement Module
function: Touchscreen cabin management console at the lead flight attendant station paired with an automated Prerecorded Announcement and Boarding Music module (PRAM). Gives cabin crew centralized control of cabin lighting scenes, zone temperature fine-tuning, potable water and waste tank level readouts, and automated safety announcements.
location: Forward Left Cabin Entry Door 1L attendant station
simple: The touchscreen control tablet mounted on the wall by the front boarding door where the lead flight attendant dims the cabin lights for takeoff, checks how full the fresh water and toilet tanks are, and triggers boarding music.

name: Cockpit Voice Recorder (CVR) & Cockpit Area Microphone
function: Crash-protected solid-state digital audio recorder painted International Orange with an attached 37.5 kHz Underwater Locator Beacon (ULB), paired with an overhead Cockpit Area Microphone (CAM). Continuously records Captain, First Officer, observer, and ambient flight-deck audio/warnings inside a titanium crash-survivable memory vault rated for 3,400 Gs and 1,100°C fires.
location: Aft unpressurized tailcone (Recorder) and Cockpit Overhead Panel (Area Mic)
simple: One of the two famous 'Black Boxes' (actually painted bright orange) bolted inside the tailcone. It records all pilot radio calls, interphone conversations, and ambient cockpit switch clicks and warning chimes.

name: HF Communication Transceiver & Antenna Coupler
function: Long-range High Frequency (2.8 to 24 MHz) single-sideband radio transceiver paired with a motorized/solid-state impedance-matching HF Antenna Coupler mounted in the leading edge or base of the vertical tailfin. Bounces radio waves off the Earth's ionosphere for beyond-line-of-sight oceanic, desert, and polar ATC communications.
location: Forward Avionics Bay (Transceiver) and Vertical Stabilizer Root (Coupler)
simple: Normal VHF radios only work line-of-sight (~200 miles). When flying across oceans or remote polar routes out of VHF range, the HF radio bounces shortwave signals off the upper atmosphere (ionosphere) to reach controllers thousands of miles away.

name: Cockpit Door Surveillance Camera System (CDSS)
function: Infrared and optical video cameras mounted in the forward cabin entry ceiling and galley area feeding a dedicated Cockpit LCD monitor. Allows pilots to visually verify the identity of anyone requesting cockpit entry and check that the forward vestibule is clear before unlocking the armored flight-deck door.
location: Forward Cabin Doorway Ceiling and Cockpit Aft Bulkhead
simple: A closed-circuit security camera and night-vision monitor system that lets the pilots see who is standing outside the armored cockpit door in the forward galley before flipping the unlock switch.

name: VHF Communication Blade Antenna
function: Aerodynamically swept vertical monopole blade antenna bonded directly to the conductive fuselage skin ground plane for VHF 1 (upper forward fuselage), VHF 2 (lower belly fuselage), and VHF 3 (upper aft fuselage) voice and digital ACARS data transmissions.
location: Upper crown and lower belly fuselage exterior skin
simple: The three shark-fin blade antennas sticking out of the top roof and bottom belly of the fuselage that transmit and receive all VHF voice calls and ACARS data messages.

name: Integrated Drive Generator (IDG)
function: Oil-cooled, hydro-mechanical Constant Speed Drive (CSD) and 90+ kVA three-phase 115/200V 400 Hz brushless AC generator integrated into a single housing and mounted via a Quick Attach-Detach (QAD) ring onto each engine's accessory gearbox. Includes a thermal/manual disconnect clutch if oil temperature exceeds limits.
location: Left and Right Engine Accessory Gearboxes
simple: A jet engine speeds up and slows down constantly between idle and takeoff power, which would make electrical frequency swing wildly. The IDG uses an internal hydraulic gear transmission to keep its generator spinning at an exact constant RPM—producing rock-steady 400 Hz electricity.

name: APU AC Generator
function: Three-phase 90+ kVA, 115/200V 400 Hz oil-cooled brushless AC generator driven directly by the Auxiliary Power Unit gearbox. Because the APU turbine runs at a constant 100% governed speed, the APU generator requires no Constant Speed Drive (CSD) and can replace either engine IDG on the ground or in flight.
location: APU Accessory Gearbox in the unpressurized tailcone
simple: The third full-size electrical generator sitting in the tailcone on the APU. Since the APU always spins at a constant 100% speed, this generator doesn't need heavy variable-speed gears and can power the entire airplane on the ground or in flight.

name: Constant Speed Motor/Generator (CSM/G — Emergency Generator)
function: Hydraulically driven 5 to 8 kVA three-phase 115/200V 400 Hz AC emergency generator powered by the emergency hydraulic system when the Ram Air Turbine (RAT) deploys into the airstream following loss of both main AC buses.
location: Belly hydraulic bay / Main Landing Gear wheel well
simple: If both main engines and the APU ever fail in flight, the drop-down Ram Air Turbine (RAT) pressurizes the emergency hydraulic system, which spins this compact hydraulic motor-generator to keep the cockpit screens and flight computers alive.

name: Main Aircraft Battery (28V Nickel-Cadmium / Lithium-Ion)
function: Heavy-duty 24V/28V DC main batteries that provide autonomous DC power for APU starting on the ground, power the Hot Battery Bus (fire squibs, parking brake, clock, fuel quantity refueling), and supply the DC Essential Bus and Static Inverter for at least 22–30 minutes during an in-flight total generator loss.
location: Forward Avionics Bay battery shelf
simple: Two rugged aviation batteries in the nose bay that start the tailcone APU when parked at a remote stand and instantly bridge power to the cockpit displays if all generators trip offline in flight.

name: Battery Charge Limiter (BCL) / Charger Controller
function: Dedicated microprocessor controller that monitors main battery voltage, charging current, and internal cell temperature. Commands the Battery Line Contactor open once charging is complete or if over-temperature / thermal runaway conditions are detected, and manages automatic battery connection during APU starting.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: Smart battery management computer that connects the batteries to the main DC bus whenever they need charging and disconnects them automatically if they get fully charged or start overheating.

name: Static Inverter (28V DC to 115V 400 Hz AC)
function: Solid-state power electronic inverter that converts 28V DC power from the aircraft batteries into constant 115V 400 Hz single-phase AC power to supply the AC Essential Bus during an all-generator loss or while the Ram Air Turbine (RAT) is deploying.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: Batteries can only store Direct Current (DC), but vital cockpit instruments need 115V 400 Hz Alternating Current (AC). The Static Inverter uses solid-state transistors to turn battery DC into 400 Hz AC with zero moving parts.

name: External / Ground Power Control Unit (GPCU / GAPCU)
function: Monitors voltage, frequency (400 Hz), and three-phase rotation sequence of any airport Ground Power Unit (GPU) plugged into the aircraft's nose external power receptacle, as well as the APU generator. Trips the External Power Contactor open immediately if the ground cart voltage or frequency drifts out of tolerance.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: Before allowing an airport ground power cart to connect to the aircraft's electrical grid, this unit checks that the incoming power is clean 115V at 400 Hz so a faulty airport cart can never fry the aircraft's electronics.

name: Generator Line Contactor (GLC) & Bus Tie Contactor (BTC)
function: Heavy-duty 260-amp three-phase electromagnetic power relays that connect or isolate the main engine generators, APU generator, and external power cart across the left and right AC main buses. Controlled automatically by the GCUs to maintain split-bus isolation in normal operation or tie buses together if one generator fails.
location: Main Electrical Power Center / Avionics Bay
simple: Giant automated electrical switches that connect the engine generators to the aircraft's power grid—and automatically click closed in milliseconds to let one working engine power both sides of the airplane if the other generator fails.

name: Three-Phase Differential Current Transformer (CT)
function: Inductive ring-core current sensors installed at both ends of the heavy generator feeder cables (inside the engine nacelle and inside the avionics bay). By comparing current leaving the generator against current arriving at the bus, the GCU detects any feeder-cable short circuit to the airframe and trips the generator within milliseconds.
location: Engine Pylon / Nacelle and Main Electrical Distribution Bay
simple: Measures the exact electrical current leaving the engine generator and compares it to the current arriving in the fuselage. If those two numbers don't match, it means a power cable shorted out in the wing, and the system cuts power instantly.

name: Generator Quick Attach-Detach (QAD) Mounting Ring
function: Precision V-band tension clamp ring and splined drive pad interface that locks the heavy Integrated Drive Generator (IDG) onto the engine accessory gearbox. Allows line mechanics to unbolt and swap a 60 kg generator using a single tension bolt without removing dozens of flange studs.
location: Engine Accessory Gearbox generator pad
simple: A clever V-grooved clamping collar that lets mechanics unbolt and swap a heavy generator off a jet engine in a fraction of the time it would take with a ring of 20 individual bolts.

name: External Ground Power Receptacle (GPU Plug Port)
function: Standardized 6-pin NATO/ISO external AC power socket recessed behind a small access door on the lower forward nose fuselage. Four thick pins carry three-phase 115/200V 400 Hz power and neutral, while two shorter interlock pins disconnect power automatically before the heavy plug can be pulled free, preventing dangerous electrical arcing.
location: Lower forward nose fuselage ahead of the nose wheel well
simple: The heavy 6-prong electrical socket under the nose where ramp crews plug in the airport's 400 Hz power cable so the airplane has full electricity at the gate with its engines and APU turned off.

name: Powered Captain & First Officer Cockpit Seats
function: Crashworthy 16G-rated flight crew seats with electric vertical/horizontal actuator motors (and manual override handles), adjustable lumbar support, folding armrests with sidestick/yoke angle scales, and a 5-point inertia-reel safety harness with crotch strap.
location: Cockpit Left (Captain) and Right (First Officer) stations
simple: The electrically adjustable cockpit seats for the Captain and First Officer, aligned with reference eye-position balls on the center windshield post so every pilot has the exact same view over the nose.

name: Cockpit Observer Seat (Jumpseat)
function: Folding or sliding cockpit observer seat with a 4- or 5-point inertia-reel harness, dedicated oxygen mask box, and third Audio Control Panel, positioned behind the center pedestal for check captains, aviation authority inspectors, or maintenance engineers.
location: Cockpit aft center or side station
simple: The folding jumpseat right behind the center console in the cockpit where check pilots, safety inspectors, or off-duty crew members sit.

name: Cockpit Sliding Window Emergency Escape Rope
function: Knotted heat-resistant braided rescue rope anchored inside a ceiling stowage locker directly above the Captain's and First Officer's sliding cockpit windows. Allows flight crew to climb out of the sliding window and lower themselves to the tarmac if the cockpit door is jammed after a ground emergency.
location: Cockpit overhead ceiling pockets above Left and Right sliding windows
simple: A heavy knotted rope tucked into a small compartment above each pilot's side window so the pilots can slide open the window and climb down to the runway if the cockpit door is blocked during an evacuation.

name: Cabin Attendant Folding Jumpseat
function: Spring-loaded auto-retracting wall- or bulkhead-mounted cabin crew seat equipped with energy-absorbing head padding, a 4-point inertia-reel harness, and an under-seat stowage compartment holding a flashlight and life vest.
location: Adjacent to forward, overwing, and aft cabin emergency exit doors
simple: The spring-loaded fold-down seats next to the exit doors where flight attendants strap in for takeoff and landing—engineered to snap flat against the wall automatically the second the attendant stands up so it never blocks an exit doorway.

name: Automatic Emergency Locator Transmitter (ELT) & Blade Antenna
function: Crash-activated tri-frequency transmitter (406 MHz digital satellite burst, 121.5 MHz civilian homing, and 243 MHz military homing) wired to a cockpit remote switch and an external dorsal fin blade antenna. Automatically triggers via an internal G-switch upon crash deceleration, beaming the aircraft's registered 24-bit hex identity and GPS coordinates to Cospas-Sarsat search-and-rescue satellites.
location: Aft cabin ceiling crown near rear fuselage and upper dorsal skin
simple: An automatic distress beacon mounted in the rear ceiling that switches itself on if it feels a crash impact—beaming the aircraft's exact identity and location straight up to search-and-rescue satellites.

name: Low-Frequency Airframe Underwater Locator Beacon (8.8 kHz ULB)
function: Long-range water-activated acoustic pinger bolted directly to the lower fuselage airframe structure. Unlike the 37.5 kHz beacons mounted on the CVR and FDR (which have a 2–3 km detection radius), this 8.8 kHz low-frequency beacon transmits an acoustic pulse detectable from 10 to 20+ kilometers away under the ocean for at least 90 days.
location: Lower fuselage structural frame
simple: While the orange black boxes carry short-range underwater pingers, modern airliners also bolt this deep-bass 8.8 kHz acoustic pinger to the fuselage frame—allowing rescue ships to hear a submerged aircraft from over 15 kilometers away!

name: Inflatable Door Escape Slide / Slide-Raft & 3,000 PSI Cylinder
function: Urethane-coated Kevlar/nylon inflatable evacuation slide (or dual-lane Slide-Raft with detachable mooring line and survival kit) vacuum-packed inside the lower cabin door bustle or wing-to-body fairing. Powered by a 3,000 psi compressed nitrogen/CO2 gas cylinder and Venturi aspirators that gulp ambient air to inflate the slide into a rigid ramp in under 3 seconds.
location: Lower bustle of each passenger entry/service door and overwing exit fairing
simple: The folded emergency slide packed inside the bottom box of every exit door. When the door is ARMED and opened, a 3,000 PSI gas bottle blasts the slide out and sucks in outside air to turn it into a rigid slide—or a floating lifeboat—in 3 seconds.

name: Overhead Cabin Life Raft Pack & Portable Survival ELT
function: Self-inflating 30-to-50-person marine canopy life raft pack, ditching survival kit (flares, sea dye, water desalinator, rations), and floating water-activated Survival Emergency Radio Beacon (ELT(S)) stowed in overhead ceiling compartments for extended overwater flights.
location: Overhead ceiling stowage compartments and attendant closets
simple: Inflatable multi-person life rafts and floating waterproof satellite distress beacons carried on overwater flights.

name: Modular Cabin Lavatory Monument
function: Self-contained honeycomb composite cabin bathroom module fitted with a pneumatic vacuum toilet assembly, sink faucet with inline electric water heater, automatic under-sink waste-bin Halon fire extinguisher bottle, ceiling smoke detector, and fold-down baby changing table.
location: Forward and Aft Passenger Cabin zones
simple: Each airplane bathroom is actually built as a single plug-and-play composite room module slid through the fuselage door during manufacturing and bolted to the floor tracks.

name: Cabin Galley Monument & Electrical Insert Bays
function: Structural composite kitchen monument anchored to the cabin floor beams to withstand 9G forward crash loads. Houses standardized ATLAS/KSSU meal-cart bays with mechanical turn-button latches, 115V 400 Hz three-phase power sockets for convection ovens and water boilers/coffee makers, and potable water shutoff valves.
location: Forward and Aft Passenger Cabin vestibules
simple: The aircraft's kitchen stations—engineered strong enough to hold hundreds of kilograms of rolling meal carts in place during turbulence and powered by 400 Hz AC outlets for ovens and espresso/coffee makers.

name: 16G Passenger Seat Triple Assembly & Floor Track Locks
function: Lightweight aluminum/carbon-fiber passenger seat row certified to withstand a 16G dynamic forward deceleration impact and a 1,038°C kerosene oil-burner fire-blocking cushion test (CS/FAR 25.853). Locks into notched extruded aluminum floor seat tracks via shear studs and anti-rattle track nuts, allowing airlines to reconfigure cabin LOPA pitch overnight.
location: Passenger Cabin main deck seat tracks
simple: Every passenger seat row is bolted into notched metal rails running the length of the floor ('Seat Tracks') and engineered with energy-absorbing legs that bend rather than snap up to 16 Gs of impact force.

name: Electrically Heated Entry Vestibule Floor Panel
function: Composite honeycomb floor panels fitted with embedded 115V AC foil heating elements and temperature sensors installed across the forward and aft passenger entry door vestibules to counteract conductive heat loss from the uninsulated metal door frames at cruise altitude.
location: Cabin floor thresholds at Forward and Aft Entry/Service Doors
simple: Because the heavy metal door frames conduct -56°C outside cold straight into the entry doorway where flight attendants stand and sit, the floor panels right inside the doors have built-in electric floor heaters!

name: Engine Fire Extinguisher Bottle & Explosive Squib Cartridge
function: Two spherical stainless-steel pressure vessels per engine (or cross-plumbed in the pylon/belly) charged with Halon 1301 (Bromotrifluoromethane) and pressurized with dry nitrogen to ~600–850 psi. Fitted with electrically fired pyrotechnic cartridges ('Squibs') that rupture a hermetic metal burst disc in milliseconds when the cockpit Agent 1 or Agent 2 button is pressed.
location: Engine Pylon or Main Landing Gear Wheel Well firewall
simple: Two heavy spherical Halon gas bottles connected to each engine. Instead of a normal valve that could leak or stick over 10 years, each bottle is sealed solid and blasted open by a tiny electric explosive cap ('squib') when the pilot fires the extinguisher.

name: APU Fire Extinguisher Bottle (With Auto-Ground Discharge)
function: Spherical Halon 1301 fire bottle mounted forward of the tailcone titanium firewall. Wired to the cockpit APU Fire panel for manual in-flight discharge, and wired to the APU ECB on the ground to trigger an automatic engine shutdown and automatic Halon bottle discharge within 3 seconds if an unmanned APU catches fire on the airport ramp.
location: Aft fuselage ahead of the APU firewall bulkhead
simple: Dedicated Halon fire bottle protecting the tailcone APU. While the plane is parked on the ground with the APU running and nobody in the cockpit, if a fire starts in the tailcone, this system automatically shuts the APU down and fires the extinguisher on its own!

name: Cargo Hold High-Rate & Low-Rate Metering Fire Bottles
function: Two-stage Class C cargo fire suppression system: Bottle 1 (High-Rate) dumps an immediate surge of Halon 1301 into the sealed forward or aft cargo hold to achieve >5% concentration knockdown, while Bottle 2 (Low-Rate) slowly meters Halon through a precision filter and pressure-reducing orifice to maintain >3% inert concentration for 60 to 240+ minutes of ETOPS diversion.
location: Under-floor belly bay adjacent to cargo compartments
simple: Fights baggage-hold fires in two steps: Bottle #1 blasts the sealed hold to knock down any open flames, and Bottle #2 slowly trickles extra Halon gas in minute-by-minute so the fire stays suffocated for up to 3+ hours while flying to an emergency airport.

name: Engine & APU Pneumatic Fire / Overheat Sensing Loops (Loop A & B)
function: Dual parallel stainless-steel sensor tubes (Loop A and Loop B) routed around the engine fan case, core combustor, turbine flange, pylon, and APU bay. Filled with pressurized helium gas and a hydrogen-charged core rod: localized fire or general overheat drives gas pressure up inside the tube, closing a diaphragm switch that signals the Fire Detection Unit (FDU).
location: Clamped around Engine 1, Engine 2, and APU nacelles/compartments
simple: Two parallel stainless-steel tripwire tubes wrapped around the hot sections of each engine. Filled with gas that expands when heated, they tell the cockpit immediately if a fuel or oil leak catches fire under the cowling—or if a hot bleed-air pipe bursts.

name: Optical Photoelectric Smoke Detector (Cargo, Lavatory & Avionics)
function: Labyrinth-chamber photoelectric smoke sensor mounted in lavatory ceilings, avionics ventilation extraction ducts, and recessed dual-loop cavities in the forward and aft cargo hold ceilings. Uses an infrared LED and photodiode offset at an angle: when smoke particles enter the chamber, they scatter light onto the photodiode and trigger cockpit smoke warnings.
location: Lavatory ceilings, Avionics extraction duct, and Cargo Hold ceiling panels
simple: Shines a hidden beam of light inside a dark labyrinth box; if smoke particles drift in, they reflect the light onto a sensor eye and trigger the cockpit smoke alarm.

name: Cockpit Engine & APU Fire Control Panel
function: Guarded emergency control panel housing the illuminated red Engine 1, Engine 2, and APU Fire switches/handles, the Agent 1 and Agent 2 squib discharge pushbuttons (with amber 'SQUIB' and 'DISCH' lights), and the Fire Loop Test button. Pulling a Fire switch cuts off fuel, hydraulics, bleed air, and generator power to that zone in one stroke.
location: Cockpit Overhead Panel or Center Pedestal
simple: The red guarded emergency switches in the cockpit. Pulling one switch completely amputates that burning engine from the aircraft—shutting off its fuel, hydraulics, bleed air, and electricity all at once—and arms the Halon fire bottles.

name: Portable Cabin Halon / Halotron & Water Fire Extinguishers
function: Handheld pressurized fire extinguishers mounted in quick-release brackets throughout the cockpit and cabin: Halon 1211 / Halotron clean-agent extinguishers for electrical, avionics, and grease fires, and antifreeze-treated Water extinguishers for cabin cloth/paper fires or cooling lithium-ion battery thermal runaway.
location: Cockpit aft wall and Cabin Attendant stations / Galley bays
simple: Handheld fire extinguishers clipped throughout the cabin and cockpit, plus specialized automatic mini fire bottles tucked underneath every bathroom trash bin that melt their own tip and spray Halon if a discarded cigarette or paper towel catches fire.

name: Spoiler Elevator Computer (SEC) / Spoiler Control Module
function: Fly-by-wire computers that command the upper-wing spoiler panels (for roll augmentation, in-flight speedbraking, and automatic ground-spoiler lift dumping on landing/RTO) and provide full standby pitch control of the elevators and horizontal stabilizer if the primary flight control computers fail.
location: Forward Avionics Bay and Aft Equipment Bay
simple: Commands the wing spoilers to pop up for turns, slowing down in the air, and dumping lift on touchdown—and acts as the instant backup computer to steer the tail elevators if the primary pitch computers ever drop offline.

name: Flight Control Data Concentrator (FCDC)
function: Dual data-acquisition computers that electrically isolate the primary flight control computers while gathering their status, control surface deflection angles, and BITE fault messages to display on the cockpit flight-control system screen and record in the maintenance computer.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
simple: Acts as a one-way digital buffer between the critical flight-control computers and the cockpit display screens so a glitch in a display screen can never feed back into the computers flying the wings.

name: Cockpit Sidestick Controller / Control Column Transducer
function: Spring-centered pilot pitch and roll input assembly equipped with dual redundant inductive (LVDT/RVDT) position transducers, an instinctive red Autopilot Disconnect / Sidestick Priority takeover button, and a solenoid lock that couples or prioritizes inputs when both pilots pull at once.
location: Cockpit Left (Captain) and Right (First Officer) stations
simple: Converts the pilot's hand movements into proportional electrical signals for the fly-by-wire computers—and includes a red thumb button that lets one pilot take 100% control if the other stick is bumped or incapacitated.

name: Trimmable Horizontal Stabilizer (THS) Ball-Screw Actuator
function: Massive high-load ball-screw jack assembly in the tailcone driven via a differential gearbox by two or three hydraulic motors (controlled electrically by the flight computers/autopilot via electric trim motors, or mechanically via the cockpit pitch-trim wheels) with dual structural load paths and no-back brakes.
location: Aft fuselage tailcone ahead of the horizontal stabilizer front spar
simple: While the small elevators on the back of the tail move up and down for quick pitch changes, this giant steel screw-jack tilts the ENTIRE horizontal tail wing up or down to keep the aircraft balanced in cruise as fuel burns off.

name: Elevator Hydraulic Servocontrol (PCU)
function: Electro-hydraulic servoactuator driving the left and right elevator surfaces for aircraft pitch control. Each elevator is powered by two independent hydraulic servocontrols; normally one actuator actively positions the surface while the second operates in hydraulic damping mode (and both automatically center the elevator to zero if all electrical control is lost).
location: Horizontal Stabilizer rear spar / elevator hinge cavity
simple: Four heavy-duty hydraulic cylinders inside the horizontal tail that move the left and right elevators up and down to pitch the aircraft's nose skyward or earthward.

name: Rudder Triple-Tandem Hydraulic Servocontrol (PCU)
function: Three independent hydraulic servoactuators (one per hydraulic system: Green, Blue, and Yellow / Left, Center, Right) mounted in parallel or tandem inside the vertical tailfin to drive the rudder simultaneously for directional yaw control, engine-out asymmetry compensation, and crosswind decrabbing.
location: Base of the Vertical Stabilizer rear spar
simple: Three powerful hydraulic actuators inside the vertical tailfin—each fed by a completely separate hydraulic system—so that even if two hydraulic systems fail completely, the pilot still has full rudder control.

name: Wing Spoiler Hydraulic Servocontrol
function: Single-acting/double-acting electro-hydraulic servoactuator mounted beneath each upper-wing spoiler panel. Distributes spoiler panels across the three hydraulic systems so that loss of any single hydraulic system leaves symmetric pairs of roll spoilers, speedbrakes, and ground spoilers fully operational.
location: Wing rear spar upper shroud box beneath each spoiler panel
simple: The hydraulic cylinder underneath each flat spoiler door on top of the wing—holding the panel locked down flush at 500 knots and popping it upward in half a second on touchdown to dump wing lift onto the wheel brakes.

name: Rudder Travel Limitation Unit (RTLU) / Ratio Changer
function: Dual-motor electromechanical variable-stop mechanism controlled by the Flight Augmentation / Air Data computers. Progressively restricts maximum rudder deflection angle from ~±30° at low takeoff/landing speeds down to ~±3.5° at high cruise speeds so aerodynamic side-loads can never overstress and snap the vertical stabilizer.
location: Base of the Vertical Stabilizer
simple: At 130 knots on the runway you need full rudder swing to fight a crosswind or a failed engine, but kicking full rudder at 500 knots in cruise would rip the tailfin off. The RTLU mechanically narrows the rudder stops as the airplane speeds up.

name: Yaw Damper Servoactuator
function: Two electro-hydraulic servoactuators pressurized by independent hydraulic systems and commanded by the Flight Augmentation / Yaw Damper computers. Automatically apply continuous small, high-rate rudder deflections to damp out swept-wing 'Dutch Roll' oscillations and coordinate turns.
location: Base of the Vertical Stabilizer fin root
simple: Swept-wing jets naturally want to wallow side-to-side in turbulence ('Dutch Roll'). The Yaw Damper actuators automatically make tiny rudder corrections every second to keep the tail riding smoothly without the pilots having to touch the pedals.

name: Rudder Trim Actuator & Artificial Feel Spring Unit
function: Dual-channel brushless DC electric rotary trim motor paired with a heavy mechanical spring artificial-feel cam box in the tailcone. Generates realistic centering force on the cockpit rudder pedals and shifts the neutral zero-force datum up to ±20° to relieve pedal leg force during single-engine flight.
location: Base of the Vertical Stabilizer
simple: Since powerful hydraulics move the rudder, the pedals in the cockpit would feel weightless without this heavy spring box—which pushes back against the pilot's feet and shifts the neutral center point when trimmed.

name: Slat & Flap Central Power Control Units (PCU)
function: Two central hydro-mechanical drive assemblies (one for Leading-Edge Slats, one for Trailing-Edge Flaps) located in the center fuselage belly. Each PCU combines two axial-piston hydraulic motors (fed by different hydraulic systems) coupled through a speed-summing differential gearbox and pressure-off brakes to spin torque shafts running out to both wingtips in 100% mechanical symmetry.
location: Main Landing Gear Wheel Well / Center Wing Box boundary
simple: Instead of putting separate motors on the left wing and right wing (which could run at different speeds and flip the plane), one central hydraulic motor box in the belly spins steel drive shafts running out into both wings simultaneously! (If one hydraulic system fails, the remaining motor still drives both wings at half speed.)

name: Slat & Flap Wing Tip Brake (WTB)
function: Hydraulically released, spring/pressure-applied multi-disc friction brake units mounted near the outboard ends of the left and right slat and flap torque-shaft transmission lines. Commanded by the SFCCs to clamp and freeze the entire drive line in milliseconds if asymmetry, runaway, overspeed, or shaft rupture is detected. Cannot be reset in flight.
location: Outboard wing slat and flap torque shaft transmission bays
simple: Emergency mechanical brakes clamped onto the flap and slat drive shafts out in the wings. If a drive shaft ever snapped inside one wing, the Wing Tip Brakes slam shut in milliseconds to freeze both wings in place before the flaps can deploy unevenly.

name: Slat/Flap Torque Shafts, Angle Gearboxes & Ball-Screw/Rotary Actuators
function: Spanwise mechanical transmission shafting, bevel gearboxes, steady bearings, and local surface actuators (linear ball-screw jacks at each trailing-edge flap track and geared rotary rack-and-pinion actuators at each leading-edge slat track) converting rotary torque from the central PCU into smooth extension and retraction.
location: Spanwise along Left and Right Wing Front and Rear Spars
simple: The 35-meter chain of spinning torque tubes, angled gearboxes, and heavy screw-jacks running inside the front and back of both wings that push the slats and flaps out along their roller tracks.

name: Asymmetry Position Pick-Off Unit (APPU) & Feedback Pick-Off Unit (FPPU)
function: Precision inductive synchro/resolver rotary sensors mounted at the far outboard tip of the left and right slat/flap torque shafts (APPU) and on the central PCU gearbox (FPPU). Continuously compare left-wing vs. right-wing shaft rotation angles for the SFCCs and cockpit flap position indicator.
location: Outboard wingtips and Central PCU gearbox in wheel well
simple: Sensors at the very tips of the left and right wings that constantly compare how far each flap shaft has turned—triggering the Wing Tip Brakes if one side lags behind the other by even a few degrees.

name: Fly-By-Wire Load Factor Accelerometers
function: Three high-precision vertical and lateral force-balance accelerometers bolted to the primary airframe keel structure near the Center of Gravity. Provide continuous real-time G-load feedback ($N_z$) to the fly-by-wire computers so Normal Law pitch control maintains exact pilot-commanded load factor and limits gusts between +2.5G and -1.0G.
location: Lower fuselage keel beam near the aircraft Center of Gravity
simple: Three G-force sensors bolted to the aircraft's structural spine that let the fly-by-wire computers feel every bump of turbulence in milliseconds and hold the airplane's vertical G-load steady.

name: Mechanical Control Cable Tension Regulator
function: Spring-loaded compensating quadrant assembly installed in the under-floor steel cable runs for the rudder and horizontal stabilizer backup controls. Automatically takes up or pays out cable slack as the aluminum fuselage contracts at -56°C in cruise (since aluminum has twice the thermal expansion coefficient of steel cable).
location: Under-floor fuselage cable run and tailcone
simple: Aluminum fuselage tubes shrink faster than steel cables when chilled to -56°C at 38,000 feet, which would make control cables go slack! This spring-loaded regulator automatically adjusts the cable loop to keep tension constant at any temperature.

name: Flap Lever & Speedbrake Lever Command Sensor Units (CSU)
function: Redundant RVDT/LVDT rotary position transducers mounted beneath the center pedestal Slat/Flap selector lever (detents 0, 1, 2, 3, FULL) and Speedbrake / Ground Spoiler control lever, converting pilot lever selections into electrical commands for the SFCCs and SECs.
location: Cockpit Center Pedestal quadrant
simple: The electronic sensors underneath the cockpit Flap Lever and Speedbrake Lever that tell the flight-control computers which flap setting the pilot just clicked into or whether the ground spoilers are armed for landing.

name: Fuel Quantity Indication Computer (FQIC)
function: Dual-channel digital processor that excites all wing and center tank capacitance probes, densitometers, and fuel temperature sensors to compute exact usable fuel mass per tank for cockpit display, automatic refueling shutoff at preselected target weight, and center-to-wing fuel transfer sequencing.
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack
simple: The master fuel calculator in the avionics bay. It gathers readings from dozens of capacitance tubes, density sensors, and thermometers inside the wings to tell the pilots their exact fuel weight in kilograms.

name: Fuel Level Sensing Control Unit (FLSCU) & Optical Level Sensors
function: Independent dual-channel controllers wired to optical/thermistor High-Level sensors (automatically closing refueling valves when a tank reaches full capacity), Low-Level sensors (triggering cockpit low-fuel cautions and opening outer-to-inner transfer valves), and Surge Tank overflow sensors.
location: Forward Avionics Bay and Wing Fuel Tanks
simple: Independent backup fuel-level safety units that watch the high-level and low-level sensors in the wings—slamming the refueling valves shut automatically if a fuel truck ever tries to overfill a wing tank.

name: Low-Pressure (LP) Fuel Shutoff Valve (Wing Spar Firewall Valve)
function: Twin-motor 28V DC rotary ball/gate valve mounted directly on the front wing spar outside the engine nacelle fire zone. Closes during normal engine shutdown via the Engine Master switch, or slams shut via an independent circuit when the red Cockpit Engine Fire switch is pulled—cutting off fuel before it enters the pylon.
location: Left and Right Wing Front Spar at engine pylon root
simple: The heavy firewall fuel shutoff valve mounted inside the wing root (away from any engine fire) that cuts off kerosene flow to the engine when shut down or when the cockpit Engine Fire handle is pulled.

name: Fuel Crossfeed Valve & Twin-Motor Actuator
function: Ball-type isolation valve driven by two independent DC electric motors inside the center wing box. Normally closed to keep Left and Right engine fuel feed manifolds completely separate; when opened by the overhead X-FEED pushbutton, interconnects both sides so either wing tank can feed both engines or correct a lateral wing fuel imbalance.
location: Center Wing Box rear spar
simple: Normally, the Left Wing feeds Engine #1 and the Right Wing feeds Engine #2. If one engine shuts down or one wing gets heavier than the other, opening the Crossfeed Valve connects both fuel pipes together so either wing can feed either engine.

name: Outer-to-Inner Fuel Transfer Valve & Defuel/Transfer Valve
function: Electrically actuated valves mounted on the rib boundary between the Outer and Inner wing tanks (and Center tank). Keep fuel weight locked out in the outer wings during takeoff and cruise for wing-bending and flutter relief, then automatically open when either inner tank drops to ~750 kg so outer-tank fuel drains inward.
location: Wing inter-tank rib boundary and center wing box
simple: Keeps several hundred kilograms of fuel trapped out near the wingtips during high-speed flight to reduce wing bending stress—then automatically opens a gate near the end of the flight to let that fuel flow inward to the engines.

name: Under-Wing Single-Point Refuel Coupling, Preselector & Refuel Valves
function: Standardized bayonet pressure-fueling coupling under the wing leading edge paired with an exterior Digital Refuel Preselector Panel and solenoid-piloted diaphragm Refuel Shutoff Valves in each tank. Allows a single fuel truck hose at 50 psi to fill all wing and center tanks automatically to the exact preselected kilogram target.
location: Wing leading edge lower access panel and tank refueling galleries
simple: The single high-pressure port and digital keypad under the wing where the fuel-truck operator dials in the Captain's requested fuel weight—letting the airplane automatically fill its outer wings first and center tank last.

name: Fuel Vent Surge Tank, Overpressure Burst Disc & NACA Flame Arrestor
function: Outboard wingtip buffer compartment connected to all fuel tanks via vent pipes and float vent valves. Breathes ambient air through a flush underside NACA ram-air scoop (keeping mild positive ram pressure on the tanks at altitude), stops outside lightning sparks with a brazen mesh flame arrestor, and includes a frangible Overpressure Protector disc if a refuel valve ever fails open.
location: Outboard Left and Right Wingtips
simple: Every fuel tank needs an air vent so it doesn't collapse like a crushed juice box as fuel is pumped out. This empty buffer tank at each wingtip lets the wing tanks breathe through a lightning-proof screen while catching any sloshing fuel.

name: Fuel Water-Scavenge Jet Pump (Venturi) & Sump Water Drain Valve
function: No-moving-parts Venturi eductor jet pump at the lowest point of each tank that uses motive fuel flow from the main boost pumps to continuously suck trace condensed water off the tank floor and entrain it into the engine feed, paired with a flush exterior Sump Water Drain Valve used by mechanics during daily walkaround fuel sampling.
location: Lowest gravity sump of Center and Inner Wing Fuel Tanks
simple: A clever Venturi suction nozzle with zero moving parts that vacuums up trace water droplets from the bottom of the fuel tank during flight so water can never pool and freeze—plus the spring-loaded belly drain valve mechanics use to test fuel with water-detector syringes.

name: APU Fuel Feed Pump & APU LP Shutoff Valve
function: Dedicated centrifugal fuel pump and motorized low-pressure isolation valve that draw fuel from the main fuel manifold and pump it all the way aft to the tailcone Auxiliary Power Unit whenever main tank boost pumps are switched off.
location: Aft Center Wing Box and Tailcone firewall boundary
simple: When an airliner first wakes up at the gate on battery power with all main wing fuel pumps turned off, this small dedicated pump pulls kerosene from the wing and pushes it back to the tailcone so the APU can start.

name: Fuel Densitometer (CADENS) & In-Tank Fuel Temperature Sensors
function: Submerged precision density transducers and thermistor temperature probes inside the wing tanks. Measure the exact density (kg/L) of each loaded fuel batch so the FQIC computes mass accurately, and display live wing fuel temperature on the cockpit fuel page to warn pilots if fuel approaches its -47°C freezing point.
location: Inner and Outer Wing Fuel Tanks
simple: Submerged sensors that measure the exact density and temperature of the kerosene inside the wings—ensuring accurate kilogram fuel readings and alerting pilots if the fuel gets close to freezing on polar flights.

name: Fuel Jettison (Fuel Dump) Pumps, Isolation Valves & WingNozzle Masts
function: High-capacity centrifugal jettison pumps and motorized wing trailing-edge dump nozzle valves installed on long-haul aircraft whose Maximum Takeoff Weight significantly exceeds Maximum Landing Weight. Rapidly discharge up to 1,500–2,500 kg/min of fuel into the slipstream to reduce landing weight in an emergency, with automaticFQIC standpipe shutoff to protect minimum reserve fuel.
location: Center/Inner Wing Tanks and Outboard Flap Track Fairing trailing-edge masts
simple: On heavy long-haul jets that take off 80 tonnes heavier than their landing gear is certified to land at, these high-speed pumps and wing nozzles spray excess fuel into the high-altitude wind so it evaporates harmlessly before an emergency landing.

name: AC Electric Motor Hydraulic Pump (EMP)
function: Three-phase 115/200V 400 Hz AC motor-driven hydraulic pump delivering 3,000 psi (or 5,000 psi) system pressure. Serves either as the primary continuous pressure source for an electrically driven hydraulic system (such as the Airbus Blue system) or as an on-demand backup/ground-service pump when main engines are shut down.
location: Belly Hydraulic Compartment / Main Wheel Well
simple: A powerful electric hydraulic pump that pressurizes the hydraulic lines to 3,000 PSI without needing the jet engines running—allowing mechanics to test flight controls or open cargo doors at the gate, and backing up the engine-driven pumps in flight.

name: Ram Air Turbine (RAT) & Emergency Pump
function: Drop-down two-bladed variable-pitch wind turbine stowed inside a belly or wing-root fairing. Automatically deploys into the slipstream via a spring/hydraulic actuator if both main AC electrical buses or all main hydraulic systems are lost in flight, spinning at several thousand RPM from wind force alone to drive an emergency hydraulic pump and emergency electrical generator.
location: Lower fuselage belly fairing or wing-to-body fairing
simple: The ultimate survival backup: a fold-out two-bladed wind turbine hidden in the belly. If both engines flame out and the plane is gliding with zero fuel, the 250-knot wind spins the RAT to power the cockpit screens and flight controls all the way to the runway.

name: Pressurized Hydraulic System Reservoir
function: Cylindrical metal reservoir tank (one per independent hydraulic system) pressurized to ~40–50 psi by engine/APU pneumatic bleed air via a Reservoir Pressurization Manifold. Houses a fluid quantity transmitter, low-level warning switch, air-pressure gauge, relief valve, and ground depressurization valve.
location: Main Landing Gear Wheel Well and Hydraulic Service Bays
simple: Separate storage tanks holding the fire-resistant hydraulic fluid for each hydraulic system—pressurized with ~45 PSI of air so the fluid never foams up or starves the high-speed pumps at 40,000 feet.

name: Hydraulic Fire Shutoff Valve (FSOV)
function: Motorized gate or ball shutoff valve installed in the low-pressure suction supply line between the hydraulic reservoir and the engine-driven hydraulic pump. Slams shut automatically when the cockpit Engine Fire handle/pushbutton is pulled, preventing hydraulic fluid from feeding an engine nacelle fire.
location: Wing Front Spar / Engine Pylon firewall boundary
simple: Stops hydraulic fluid from flowing out of the wing tank into the engine pump the instant a pilot pulls the red Engine Fire switch.

name: Hydraulic System Pressure Accumulator
function: Spherical or cylindrical bladder/diaphragm pressure vessel pre-charged with dry nitrogen gas (typically ~1,885 psi on a 3,000 psi system). Absorbs sudden hydraulic pressure spikes ('water hammer') and supplies instantaneous pressurized fluid volume when fast-acting flight control actuators move before the variable-displacement pump swashplate can react.
location: Hydraulic System Bays and Wheel Well
simple: A nitrogen-cushioned metal sphere in each hydraulic system that smooths out pressure ripples and provides an instant burst of 3,000 PSI fluid when multiple flight controls move at once.

name: Hydraulic Priority Valve
function: Spring-loaded hydro-mechanical pressure-sequencing valve that automatically cuts off hydraulic flow to heavy, high-volume secondary users (such as Landing Gear retraction, Slats, Flaps, and Nose Wheel Steering) if system pressure drops below ~1,800 psi—preserving all remaining hydraulic pressure for primary flight controls.
location: High-Pressure Hydraulic Manifolds in Wheel Well / Belly Bay
simple: If a pump is struggling and hydraulic pressure drops low, the Priority Valve automatically cuts off heavy power-hungry gear and flap motors so the elevators, rudder, and ailerons keep 100% of the remaining pressure.

name: High-Pressure, Case-Drain & Return Hydraulic Filter Manifold
function: Integrated aluminum manifold block fitted with replaceable 3-to-5-micron pleated filter elements and pop-out red differential-pressure ('clogging') indicator buttons. Traps microscopic metallic wear debris from pumps and actuators before it can contaminate the system or jam flight-control electro-hydraulic servovalves.
location: Hydraulic Service Bays and Engine Nacelles
simple: Ultra-fine micron filters that scrub the hydraulic fluid clean on every single pass—fitted with a little red button that pops out if the filter starts clogging so mechanics spot it during their walkaround.

name: Ground Service Manual Hydraulic Hand Pump
function: Single-cylinder lever-operated manual piston pump installed inside the hydraulic ground service panel. Allows ground crew to manually pump hydraulic fluid from the reservoir to open or close the Forward and Aft Cargo Doors when the aircraft has zero electrical power and no Ground Power Unit available.
location: Lower fuselage belly hydraulic ground service panel
simple: If an airplane is parked on a dark tarmac with dead batteries and no ground power truck, a ramp mechanic can insert a long handle into this manual hand pump and jack the heavy belly cargo doors open by hand!

name: Hydraulic Pressure Transducer, Low-Pressure Switch & Overheat Sensor
function: Manifold-mounted piezoelectric pressure transducers (sending live 0–3,000 psi readings to the cockpit hydraulic display), low-pressure switches (triggering amber warnings below ~1,450 psi), and reservoir/pump case-drain thermistor temperature sensors (triggering overheat warnings above ~95°C).
location: Hydraulic High-Pressure Manifolds and Reservoirs
simple: Sensors on all three hydraulic systems that display live PSI pressure on the cockpit screen and immediately alert the pilots if pressure drops low or if the fluid starts overheating.

name: Hydraulic System Relief Valve & Ground Leak-Measurement Valves
function: Spring-loaded high-pressure system Relief Valves (cracking open at ~3,400–3,500 psi to protect pipes if a pump pressure regulator sticks) and electrically controlled Ground Leak-Measurement Solenoid Valves that let mechanics isolate individual wing or tail branches from the cockpit maintenance panel to troubleshoot internal actuator leaks.
location: Belly Hydraulic Manifolds
simple: Includes the safety pop-off valve that prevents a runaway pump from bursting the hydraulic pipes at 3,500 PSI, plus zone shutoff valves that let mechanics isolate one wing at a time to find a leaky actuator.

name: Window Heat Computer (WHC) / Controller
function: Dual solid-state controllers (Left and Right) that regulate 115V/200V AC electrical heating power to the transparent conductive Indium-Tin-Oxide / gold coating inside the front cockpit windshields and side windows. Uses embedded thermistor feedback to hold window temperature around +35°C to +43°C for anti-icing, defogging, and bird-strike PVB vinyl elasticity.
location: Forward Avionics Bay
