simple: Regulates the electricity flowing through the invisible heating film inside the cockpit windows so they stay ice-free, fog-free, and warm enough (~40°C) to stretch and absorb a bird strike without shattering.

name: Wing Anti-Ice (WAI) Shutoff & Pressure Regulating Valve
function: Electrically controlled, pneumatically actuated butterfly valve mounted inside each wing leading edge. When the cockpit Wing Anti-Ice switch is turned ON in flight, opens and regulates hot pneumatic bleed air into perforated aluminum/titanium 'piccolo' tubes running inside the outboard leading-edge slats, then exhausts the air through under-slat slots.
location: Left and Right Wing Leading Edge root
simple: When flying through icy clouds, opening this valve blasts hot 200°C engine bleed air through perforated 'piccolo' pipes inside the front edge of the wings to keep ice from forming on the leading edges.

name: Engine Air Intake (Nacelle) Anti-Ice Valve
function: Solenoid-controlled, pneumatically actuated butterfly valve (or mechanical override valve) that taps hot compressor air from the engine core and routes it into the 360-degree D-duct inside the engine inlet cowl lip. prevents ice build-up that could break off into the spinning fan blades, and is engineered 'fail-safe open' if electrical control power is lost.
location: Left and Right Engine Core / Fan Cowl boundary
simple: Keeps the shiny metal nose lip at the front of each jet engine hot so ice can never build up and get sucked into the fan blades—and is built with a spring that pushes it OPEN automatically if its electrical wire ever breaks!

name: Electronic Ice Detector Probe & Lighted Visual Ice Indicator
function: Dual magnetostrictive ultrasonic vibrating-rod sensors on the lower forward nose (whose resonant frequency drops when 0.5 mm of ice accretes, triggering cockpit icing alerts and melting the rod clean to repeat the cycle) paired with an externally lighted Visual Ice Indicator peg mounted between the front windshields.
location: Forward nose fuselage exterior skin and center windshield post
simple: Electronic probes under the nose that vibrate at ultrasonic frequency to detect a half-millimeter coat of ice automatically, backed up by a simple lighted metal peg sticking out right between the front windshields that pilots can check with their own eyes.

name: Cockpit Windshield Wiper Motor-Converter & Arm Assembly
function: Two completely independent two-speed (LOW / HIGH) electric rotary-to-oscillating wiper motor-converters driving high-downforce spring-loaded wiper arms across the Captain's and First Officer's front windshields during takeoff, approach, and landing in heavy precipitation.
location: Forward nose cowling directly beneath Captain and First Officer windshields
simple: Independent heavy-duty windshield wiper motors built to sweep torrential rain off the cockpit glass against a 230-knot (425 km/h) headwind without lifting off the glass.

name: Electrically Heated Grey-Water Drain Mast
function: Aerodynamic airfoil-shaped fairing and internal stainless-steel pipe protruding from the forward and aft lower fuselage belly, heated by self-regulating electrical elements controlled by a Drain Mast Control Unit. Discharges lavatory sink and galley drain water ('grey water') into the slipstream as a fine mist without freezing into dangerous ice blocks at -56°C.
location: Forward and Aft lower fuselage belly centerline
simple: Aerodynamic heated metal fins sticking out of the bottom of the airplane's belly that vaporize soapy bathroom-sink and kitchen drain water into a fine mist so it never freezes into giant icicles at 38,000 feet.

name: Display Management Computer (DMC) / Symbol Generator
function: Three high-speed graphics processors (DMC 1, DMC 2, and hot-standby DMC 3) that acquire flight, navigation, weather radar, and engine data from the ADIRUs, FMGCs, and SDACs and render real-time symbology onto all six Cockpit Display Units (PFD, ND, Upper and Lower ECAM/EICAS).
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack
simple: The three 'graphics cards' in the avionics bay that draw the artificial horizon, moving map, and engine gauges onto the six cockpit screens—with a full third computer waiting on hot standby to take over at the flip of a switch.

name: System Data Acquisition Concentrator (SDAC)
function: Dual data concentrators that convert hundreds of analog discrete, synchro, and pressure/temperature sensor signals from hydraulic, fuel, pneumatic bleed, electrical, oxygen, and door systems into digital ARINC 429 data words for the Display Management Computers (system pages) and Flight Warning Computers (amber cautions).
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack
simple: Collects hundreds of analog sensor voltages, switch positions, and pressures from all over the airplane and translates them into digital data so the cockpit screens can draw live system diagrams.

name: ECAM / EICAS Display Control Panel (ECP)
function: Center pedestal control panel featuring display brightness knobs, the Takeoff Configuration (T.O CONFIG) test button, Emergency Cancel button, CLR / RCL / STS checklist keys, and dedicated system page pushbuttons (ENG, BLEED, PRESS, ELEC, HYD, FUEL, APU, COND, DOOR, WHEEL, F/CTL).
location: Cockpit Center Pedestal forward console
simple: The button pad on the center console where pilots or mechanics press 'HYD', 'FUEL', 'ELEC', or 'DOOR' to pull up live schematic diagrams of any aircraft system on the lower center screen—and press 'CLR' to step through electronic checklists.

name: Central Maintenance Computer (CMC) / CFDIU
function: Dual-channel onboard maintenance diagnostic computer that interrogates the Built-In Test Equipment (BITE) of more than 60 aircraft LRUs across all ATA chapters. Correlates cockpit warning effects with underlying root-cause LRU fault codes, generates the Post-Flight Report (PFR) after engine shutdown, and enables interactive BITE ground testing via the MCDU.
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack
simple: The master diagnostic computer for aircraft mechanics. After every flight, it compiles a 'Post-Flight Report' pairing every warning light the pilots saw with the exact black-box computer fault code that caused it.

name: Flight Data Interface and Management Unit (FDIMU / DFDAU)
function: Combined Digital Flight Data Acquisition Unit (DFDAU) and Data Management Unit (DMU). Formats mandatory flight parameters for the crash-protected Flight Data Recorder (FDR), writes high-rate FOQA/FDM data to the Quick Access Recorder (QAR), and triggers automated maintenance Load Reports (such as Hard Landing or Engine Exceedance printouts).
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack
simple: The master data logger that feeds both the orange crash recorder in the tail and the airline's daily health-monitoring system—and automatically prints out a Hard Landing report on the cockpit printer if touchdown G-limits are crossed.

name: Solid-State Flight Data Recorder (FDR) & Triaxial Accelerometer
function: Crash-hardened flight parameter recorder painted International Orange with a 90-day 37.5 kHz Underwater Locator Beacon (ULB), paired with a triaxial Linear Accelerometer at the aircraft's Center of Gravity. Records 1,000 to 3,000+ continuous flight, control-surface, and engine parameters for at least 25 hours inside a titanium crash-survivable memory module.
location: Aft unpressurized tailcone (FDR) and Center of Gravity keel beam (Accelerometer)
simple: The second famous 'Black Box' (painted bright orange) in the tailcone: logs thousands of continuous engineering measurements—every control movement, altitude, airspeed, G-load, and engine RPM—inside a fireproof titanium vault.

name: Wireless Quick Access Recorder (WQAR / QAR)
function: Unarmored solid-state data recorder with integrated 4G/5G cellular and airport Wi-Fi transceivers mounted in the avionics bay. Records raw high-resolution flight parameters from the FDIMU onto removable/internal flash memory and automatically uploads the encrypted flight file to the airline's Flight Data Monitoring (FDM / FOQA) and CAMO servers upon gate arrival.
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack
simple: The everyday sister to the orange black box: as soon as the airplane touches down and parks at the gate, the WQAR connects over cellular or airport Wi-Fi and beams the entire flight's performance data straight to the airline's safety and engineering offices.

name: Cockpit Thermal Multipurpose Printer
function: High-speed 80-column thermal paper roll printer mounted in the center pedestal. Prints ACARS pre-departure ATC clearances, digital ATIS weather, final Weight & Balance Loadsheets, CFDIU Post-Flight Maintenance Reports (PFRs), and FDIMU hard-landing/engine Load Reports.
location: Cockpit Center Pedestal aft console
simple: The thermal paper printer between the pilots' seats that spits out digital weather briefings, final loadsheets before pushback, and automated maintenance fault reports after landing.

name: Cockpit Digital Master Clock / Chronometer
function: Precision quartz/GPS-synchronized master clock with internal battery backup on the main instrument panel. Provides an independent Elapsed Time flight counter, approach stopwatch chronometer, and the master UTC date and time reference broadcast across all aircraft computers, the Flight Data Recorder, and fault logs.
location: Cockpit Main Instrument Panel
simple: More than just a dashboard clock for the pilots: this unit is the master UTC timekeeper that timestamps every single fault code, ACARS message, and black-box recording across the entire aircraft.

name: Avionics Data Loading Selector (DLRB) & Data Loader Port
function: Cockpit rotary selector switch, routing box, and high-speed ARINC 615 / Ethernet data-loader receptacle used by avionics engineers to upload 28-day FMS navigation databases, display software, and operational flight programs into target computers across the avionics bay.
location: Cockpit Pedestal / Overhead Panel and Forward Avionics Bay
simple: Every 28 days, global airway routes and runway procedures are updated worldwide. Instead of unbolting computers in the belly, engineers plug a laptop/data-loader into this cockpit port to upload fresh navigation databases and software straight into the aircraft!

name: Main Landing Gear (MLG) Leg & Oleo-Pneumatic Shock Strut
function: Primary load-bearing landing gear assembly forged from ultra-high-strength steel (such as 300M) and titanium. Comprises the outer Main Fitting barrel, chrome-plated inner Sliding Piston (filled with compressed dry nitrogen and mineral hydraulic oil to absorb touchdown sink-rate energy up to 10 ft/sec), Side Stay, Lock Stay, and Wheel Axle / Bogie Beam. Overhauled on a strict 10-to-12-year Hard-Time clock.
location: Left and Right Wing Rear Spar / Main Gear Wheel Well
simple: The massive forged steel legs under the wings that absorb the hammer blow of touchdown using an internal cushion of compressed nitrogen and oil, then fold sideways inward into the central belly bay after takeoff.

name: Nose Landing Gear (NLG) Leg, Oleo Strut & Drag Brace
function: Forward-retracting twin-wheel shock-strut assembly comprising the outer Main Barrel, chrome-plated Sliding Piston with internal centering cams (which mechanically force the nosewheels straight ahead as the strut extends after liftoff), folding Drag Brace, and integral hydraulic steering actuator.
location: Forward Fuselage Nose Wheel Well below cockpit
simple: The front steerable landing gear leg under the cockpit nose. It folds forward into the nose bay—so if hydraulic power ever fails, unlocking it lets both gravity and the 200-knot wind push the leg down and lock it into place!

name: MLG Retraction Actuator, Folding Side Stay & Downlock Springs
function: Heavy double-acting hydraulic cylinder that swings the Main Landing Gear leg inward into the belly wheel well, paired with the two-piece folding Side Stay, Lock Stay Actuator, and dual tension Downlock Springs that snap the side stay 'over-center' into a rigid geometric triangle when extended.
location: Main Landing Gear bays Left and Right
simple: The hydraulic cylinder that lifts the heavy main wheels up into the belly after takeoff, plus the geometric folding side-brace that locks 'over-center' into a rigid triangle on landing so sideloads can never collapse the leg.

name: Landing Gear & Gear Door Mechanical Uplock Boxes
function: Spring-loaded mechanical hook-and-latch boxes bolted to the nose and main wheel-well ceilings. Mechanically catch and hold the landing gear and main gear door rollers once retracted so hydraulic pressure can be shut off during cruise; unlocked hydraulically for normal extension or tripped mechanically by the Gravity Extension system.
location: Nose and Main Landing Gear Wheel Well ceilings
simple: Once the heavy landing gear folds up into the belly, you don't want to keep hydraulic cylinders pressurized for a 10-hour flight. This steel claw catches a roller pin on the gear leg and holds it up mechanically until approach.

name: Landing Gear Gravity (Free-Fall) Extension Crank & Actuator
function: Independent emergency gear-extension mechanism actuated by a fold-out crank handle (or electric free-fall switch) on the cockpit floor/pedestal. Simultaneously opens hydraulic vent/bypass valves (letting trapped fluid circulate freely) and mechanically releases the door and gear uplock hooks so the nose and main gears drop under gravity and lock via air loads and downlock springs.
location: Cockpit Center Pedestal / Floor and Main Wheel Well bulkhead
simple: Connected to the emergency crank handle in the cockpit: if the primary hydraulic system loses all fluid, turning this crank vents the hydraulic lines and trips the uplock claws so all three landing gears drop and lock by gravity alone.

name: Normal & Alternate Brake Servovalve Manifolds & ABCU
function: Electro-hydraulic proportional brake-pressure metering servovalves on the Normal and Alternate hydraulic systems, backed by an Alternate Braking Control Unit (ABCU). Modulate hydraulic pressure to each individual wheel brake up to 100 times per second to prevent tyre skidding and locked-wheel blowouts.
location: Forward Avionics Bay (ABCU) and Main Wheel Well / Gear Struts (Servovalves)
simple: High-speed hydraulic valves and backup brake electronics that pulse brake pressure on and off dozens of times per second on slippery runways so a skidding wheel instantly recovers grip.

name: Brake Hydraulic Accumulator, Parking Brake Valve & Triple Indicator
function: Nitrogen-precharged hydraulic bladder accumulator paired with an electrically operated Parking Brake Shutoff Valve and a cockpit Triple Pressure Indicator gauge (showing Accumulator pressure, Left Brake pressure, and Right Brake pressure). Guarantees at least 12 hours of parking brake clamping at the gate and at least 7 full manual brake applications in flight if all hydraulic pumps fail.
location: Main Landing Gear Wheel Well and Cockpit Center Instrument Panel
simple: A pressurized storage sphere that holds backup hydraulic pressure for the wheel brakes—keeping the parking brake clamped tight overnight and giving the pilots at least 7 full brake pedal stops even if every pump on the plane is dead.

name: Main Wheel Electric Brake Cooling Fan & Wheel-Speed Tachometer
function: Hub-mounted 115V AC axial impeller fan and pulse Wheel-Speed Tachometer Generator installed inside each main landing gear axle. The tachometer measures instant wheel spin-up (>60–72 knots for ground-spoiler logic) and skid deceleration for anti-skid; the fan pulls ambient air across the hot carbon brake pack at the gate to slash turnaround cooling time.
location: Inside Main Landing Gear Wheel Hubs / Axles
simple: Tucked right inside each main wheel hub is a speed sensor that tells the computer the exact millisecond the tyres spin up on landing, plus a high-speed electric fan that blows air through the glowing carbon brakes at the gate so the plane can take off again in 25 minutes.

name: Brake Temperature Monitoring Unit (BTMU) & Carbon Brake Thermocouples
function: Chromel-Alumel thermocouple probes embedded inside each main wheel carbon brake stator stack feeding a strut-mounted Brake Temperature Monitoring Unit (BTMU). Converts millivolt heat signals into digital temperatures displayed on the cockpit wheel page, triggering an amber BRAKE HOT caution above 300°C.
location: Main Landing Gear Brake Packs and Gear Strut
simple: Reads the temperature sensors buried inside each carbon brake stack and sends the exact degrees Celsius up to the cockpit screen so pilots know if the brakes are cool enough to retract safely into the wheel well after takeoff.

name: Nose Wheel Steering Handwheel (Tiller) & Rack-and-Pinion Actuator
function: Side-console steering handwheels (Tillers) beside the Captain and First Officer seats wired via the BSCU to an electro-hydraulic rack-and-pinion or push-pull steering actuator collar on the Nose Landing Gear. Provides up to ±75° low-speed taxi steering via the tiller and ±6° high-speed runway steering via the rudder pedals, plus a towing bypass valve.
location: Cockpit Side Consoles (Tiller) and Nose Landing Gear Upper Barrel (Actuator)
simple: Airliners don't use the control yoke to steer on the ground—instead, pilots steer around sharp airport taxiway corners using a small D-shaped 'Tiller' handle beside their knee that commands hydraulic cylinders on the nose gear.

name: Landing Gear Torque Links (Scissor Links) & Hydraulic Shimmy Damper
function: Hinged Upper and Lower forged steel/titanium scissor arms connecting the outer shock-strut cylinder to the inner sliding piston, paired with a hydraulic damping cylinder across the apex pin. Prevents the inner piston and wheels from rotating out of alignment while allowing vertical strut compression, and damps high-frequency wheel 'shimmy' oscillations during high-speed rollout.
location: Front or Rear face of Nose and Main Landing Gear shock struts
simple: The V-shaped 'scissor arms' on each landing gear leg. Without them, the round inner shock-absorber tube would spin freely like a shopping-cart wheel instead of pointing straight down the runway!

name: Landing Gear High-Speed Safety Cut-Out Valve & Brake Pedal Transmitters
function: An electrically controlled hydraulic Safety Cut-Out Valve that automatically isolates all 3,000 psi hydraulic pressure from the landing gear circuit above ~260 knots (so accidental movement of the gear lever in cruise cannot open the gear doors), plus under-floor LVDT Brake Pedal Transmitter Units converting pilot toe-pedal depression into electrical brake commands.
location: Main Wheel Well Hydraulic Bay and Under-Cockpit Floor
simple: Includes the high-speed safety valve that locks out landing gear hydraulics above 260 knots in flight, and the electronic sensors under the cockpit rudder pedals that measure how hard pilots press their toe brakes.

name: Forged Split-Rim Wheel Hub, Fusible Plugs & Nitrogen Radial Tyre
function: Two-piece forged aluminum wheel rim bolted together with high-strength tie bolts, fitted with an inflation valve, overpressure burst disc, and thermal eutectic Fusible Plugs (which melt at ~177°C–200°C to deflate the tyre safely before extreme brake heat can explode it), mounting a tubeless multi-ply nylon/aramid aircraft tyre inflated to ~180–220 psi with dry nitrogen.
location: Nose and Main Landing Gear axles
simple: Aircraft wheels are bolted together in two halves so mechanics can mount the rock-hard 200-PSI tyres—and each main wheel rim has tiny lead-alloy 'fusible plugs' that melt if the brakes overheat, hissing the nitrogen out safely so the tyre never explodes.

name: Main Wing-Root Landing Lights
function: High-intensity 600W halogen or high-output LED floodlight assemblies mounted in the inboard left and right wing roots (either fixed behind aerodynamic glass lenses or electrically retractable into the lower wing belly). Controlled from the cockpit overhead panel to illuminate the runway approach and touchdown zone at night.
location: Inboard Left and Right Wing Root leading edge or lower belly fairing
simple: The aircraft's main high-beam headlights tucked into the wing roots, powerful enough to light up an entire runway from half a mile away on final approach.

name: Nose Gear Taxi, Takeoff & Runway Turnoff Lights
function: Forward spotlight cluster mounted on the non-rotating barrel of the Nose Landing Gear strut: a wide-beam Taxi Light, a narrow high-intensity Takeoff Light, and left/right 45°-to-50°-angled Runway Turnoff Lights that illuminate curved high-speed taxiway exits. Automatically extinguish when the nose gear is retracted.
location: Nose Landing Gear strut barrel
simple: Cluster of headlights bolted right onto the front nose gear leg: straight beams for taxiing and rolling down the runway, plus two angled side lights that illuminate dark taxiway turnoffs.

name: Navigation (Position) Lights & White Anti-Collision Strobe Lights
function: Mandatory exterior position and anti-collision lights: steady Red on the Left Wingtip (110° forward arc), steady Green on the Right Wingtip (110° forward arc), and steady White on the Tailcone (140° aft arc), paired with high-voltage capacitor-discharge xenon or high-output LED White Strobe Lights at both wingtips and the tailcone.
location: Left Wingtip, Right Wingtip, and extreme Aft Tailcone tip
simple: By international aviation law, every plane wears a steady Red light on its left wingtip, a Green light on its right wingtip, and a White light on its tail—so other pilots at night can tell instantly which way you are flying—plus bright white strobe flashes.

name: Upper & Lower Red Rotating / LED Anti-Collision Beacon Lights
function: Two red high-intensity flashing LED or xenon beacon units mounted at the highest point of the fuselage roof crown and the lowest point of the center wing-box belly. Switched ON by the pilots immediately prior to engine start or pushback and kept ON until engines finish spooling down at the arrival gate.
location: Upper fuselage roof crown and lower center fuselage belly
simple: The flashing red lights on the top and bottom of the fuselage. On the airport ramp, a flashing red beacon is the universal warning signal telling ground crew: 'Stay clear—the jet engines are running or about to start!'

name: Wing / Engine Ice Inspection Lights & Tail Fin Logo Lights
function: Flush-mounted spotlights recessed into the left and right forward fuselage sides aimed backward onto the wing leading edges and engine intakes so flight crew can visually inspect for ice accumulation at night, plus floodlights mounted in the upper surface of the horizontal stabilizer that illuminate the vertical tailfin airline logo below 10,000 feet.
location: Forward fuselage sides ahead of wings and Horizontal Stabilizer upper surfaces
simple: Spotlights built into the sides of the fuselage that shine onto the front edge of the wings and engines so pilots can check for ice at night, plus floodlights on the horizontal tail that light up the airline's tail logo.

name: Emergency Lighting Power Supply Unit (EPSU) & Overwing Escape Lights
function: Self-contained rechargeable NiCd battery and inverter packs distributed above the cabin ceiling. Automatically energize interior EXIT signs, aisle ceiling floodlights, floor-proximity escape path lighting strips, and exterior Overwing & Door Slide Floodlights for at least 10–15 minutes if normal aircraft AC power fails or when switched on from the cockpit/FAP.
location: Cabin ceiling crown racks and exterior fuselage skin around overwing exits
simple: Dedicated backup battery packs hidden in the cabin ceiling that automatically light up the aisle floor strips, EXIT signs, and outside wing escape routes during a dark emergency evacuation.

name: Air Data Module (ADM — Remote Pitot/Static Pressure Transducer)
function: Remote high-precision pressure transducer LRU mounted right inside the forward fuselage skin adjacent to each Pitot Probe and Flush Static Port. Converts raw pneumatic total or static air pressure directly into digital ARINC 429 data words for the three ADIRUs—eliminating long, laggy pneumatic instrument tubing behind the cockpit.
location: Forward under-floor avionics/nose bay adjacent to pitot and static ports
simple: Instead of running long air tubes from the nose probes all the way to the cockpit gauges, each Pitot tube and Static port connects to an Air Data Module right inside the nose wall that turns air pressure into digital computer signals on the spot.

name: Flush Static Pressure Port & RVSM Critical Skin Zone
function: Electrically heated, mirror-smooth flush metal plate with small radial pressure-sensing orifices riveted seamlessly into the left and right forward fuselage skin inside a painted 'RVSM Critical Area' boundary. Measures undisturbed ambient atmospheric Static Pressure ($P_s$) for barometric altimetry, vertical speed, and airspeed calculation.
location: Forward fuselage exterior skin, Left and Right sides (Captain, F/O, and Standby)
simple: Flush metal sensor plates on the sides of the nose that measure the outside atmospheric air pressure to calculate the plane's altitude—surrounded by a strict 'DO NOT PAINT / NO DENTS' box so bumps don't distort the airflow.

name: Total Air Temperature (TAT) Sensor Probe
function: Electrically anti-iced, boundary-layer-diverting scoop probe containing dual platinum resistance thermometer windings. Measures stagnation Total Air Temperature (ambient air heated by adiabatic compression at flight Mach number) to feed the Air Data Computers (calculating True Airspeed and Static Air Temperature) and Engine FADECs.
location: Forward lower nose fuselage exterior skin
simple: A specially shaped metal thermometer scoop under the nose that measures the temperature of air crashing into the plane at 500 mph—allowing the computers to calculate true outside temperature and engine thrust limits.

name: Integrated Standby Instrument System (ISIS) & Standby Magnetic Compass
function: Self-contained solid-state LCD standby flight instrument incorporating its own internal MEMS gyroscopes, accelerometers, and direct pitot/static pressure ports, paired with a liquid-damped whiskey Standby Magnetic Compass on the center windshield post. Provides independent Attitude, Airspeed, Altitude, and ILS approach guidance on battery power if all 3 ADIRUs or all 6 main displays fail.
location: Cockpit Center Main Instrument Panel and Center Windshield Post
simple: The ultimate independent backup instrument in the middle of the dashboard: wired directly to the aircraft battery and its own air tubes so that even if every main computer screen goes black, pilots still have a working artificial horizon, airspeed, and altimeter.

name: Multi-Mode Receiver (MMR — ILS, GPS & GLS) & Active GPS Antennas
function: Dual precision navigation receivers fed by top-mounted Active Satellite GPS Antennas and nose-radome Localizer (VHF) and Glideslope (UHF) antennas. Computes high-integrity GPS position, velocity, and UTC time for ADIRU hybrid inertial alignment, and decodes CAT III ILS Localizer/Glideslope radio beams for automatic landing.
location: Forward Avionics Bay (MMR), Upper Fuselage Crown (GPS Antenna), and Nose Radome (ILS Antennas)
simple: Combines high-precision satellite GPS navigation with the runway Instrument Landing System (ILS) radio receivers inside one unit—guiding the airplane across continents and right down onto the runway centerline in zero-visibility fog.

name: Radio Altimeter (RA) Transceiver & Flush Belly Antennas
function: Dual frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) 4.3 GHz C-band radar altimeters connected to flush transmit and receive patch antennas on the aft lower fuselage belly. Measure exact physical wheel height Above Ground Level (AGL) from 2,500 feet down to touchdown for GPWS terrain protection, synthetic voice callouts ('FIFTY, THIRTY, RETARD'), and CAT III Autoland flare.
location: Aft Under-Floor Cargo Bay and Lower Fuselage Belly Skin
simple: Barometric altimeters only measure air pressure above sea level. Below 2,500 feet, these two radar boxes bounce radio waves straight off the ground underneath the belly to measure exact wheel height down to the foot for automatic landing flares.

name: Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning Computer (EGPWC / TAWS)
function: Terrain Awareness and Warning System computer containing a worldwide digital terrain, obstacle, and runway elevation database. Compares aircraft GPS/IRS position, radio altitude, vertical sink rate, and gear/flap configuration to display color-coded terrain maps on the Navigation Display and trigger 'TERRAIN, TERRAIN — PULL UP!' or 'SINK RATE' voice alerts.
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack
simple: Stores a 3D topographical map of every mountain, hill, and runway on Earth. If an airplane in clouds ever descends toward high ground or approaches a runway without its wheels down, the EGPWC flashes a red map and shouts 'PULL UP!'

name: Weather Radar (WXR) Transceiver, Stabilized Flat-Plate Antenna & Mount
function: X-band (~9.3 GHz) pulse-Doppler weather radar transceiver driving a pitch-and-roll stabilized motorized planar array antenna dish inside the nose radome. Detects precipitation reflectivity (Green, Amber, Red, Magenta), measures horizontal droplet velocity shifts for Turbulence detection, and scans ahead below 1,500 feet for microburst Predictive Windshear (PWS).
location: Nose Radome Bay (Antenna & Mount) and Forward Avionics Bay (Transceiver)
simple: The motorized radar dish hidden inside the fiberglass nosecone. It scans 320 nautical miles ahead for thunderstorm rain cores and uses the Doppler shift of moving raindrops to warn pilots of dangerous windshear on final approach.

name: ATC Mode S Transponder (ADS-B Out) & ATC/TCAS Control Panel
function: Dual air traffic surveillance transponders controlled via a center-pedestal ATC/TCAS Control Unit and wired to top and bottom fuselage blade antennas. Replies to ground secondary radar and airborne TCAS interrogations with the 4-digit squawk code, barometric altitude, 24-bit ICAO aircraft address, and automatic 1090 MHz ADS-B Out GPS position/velocity broadcasts.
location: Forward Avionics Bay and Cockpit Center Pedestal
simple: Broadcasts the aircraft's callsign, exact GPS position, speed, and altitude once per second to Air Traffic Control radar screens, nearby TCAS aircraft, and public flight-tracking receivers.

name: VOR Receiver, DME Interrogator, Marker Beacon & ADF Receiver
function: Ground-beacon radio navigation suite: dual VHF Omnidirectional Range (VOR, 108.00–117.95 MHz) receivers computing magnetic bearing radials; dual UHF Distance Measuring Equipment (DME) transceivers measuring slant-range distance in nautical miles by pulse round-trip time; 75 MHz Marker Beacon receiver; and Automatic Direction Finder (ADF).
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack with antennas on belly and vertical tailfin
simple: Classic ground-beacon radio receivers that continuously cross-check the aircraft's position by measuring exact compass bearings (VOR) and round-trip radio pulse distances (DME) to ground stations along the route.

name: Flight Crew High-Pressure Oxygen Cylinder & Pressure Regulator
function: Composite-overwrapped or steel high-pressure cylinder charged to ~1,850 psi with dry Aviator's Breathing Oxygen, fitted with a combined High-Pressure Regulator/Transducer, Crew Supply Solenoid Valve, and green overboard thermal discharge indicator disc. Steps bottle pressure down to ~70–85 psi for the cockpit quick-donning mask boxes.
location: Forward Avionics Bay / Lower Nose Compartment
simple: High-pressure gaseous oxygen bottles in the forward nose bay dedicated strictly to the cockpit pilots—monitored on the cockpit system display before every flight.

name: Cockpit Quick-Donning Diluter-Demand Oxygen Mask & Stowage Box
function: Full-face or oro-nasal mask with integrated smoke goggles, boom microphone, and 3-mode regulator (NORMAL diluter-demand, 100% pure oxygen, and EMERGENCY positive pressure). Squeezing the red release paddles inflates the tubular rubber head harness with 70 psi oxygen so a pilot can don it one-handed in under 5 seconds.
location: Cockpit Left, Right, and Observer side consoles
simple: The pilot's emergency oxygen and smoke mask. Squeezing two red paddles inflates the head straps like a bicycle inner tube so it slips over a pilot's glasses and headset with one hand in 3 seconds, then deflates tight to seal out cockpit smoke.

name: Passenger PSU Chemical Oxygen Generator & Drop-Down Mask Container
function: Overhead Passenger Service Unit (PSU) container housing 2, 3, or 4 yellow continuous-flow oxygen masks and a solid-state Sodium Chlorate ($NaClO_3$) and Iron powder Chemical Oxygen Generator. Unlatched electrically if cabin altitude exceeds 14,000 ft; pulling any mask lanyard pulls a firing pin that ignites the chemical core to produce breathable oxygen for 12–22 minutes.
location: Overhead Passenger Service Units above every seat row, lavatory, and galley
simple: The overhead compartment above every seat row holding the yellow oxygen masks and a 15-minute chemical 'oxygen candle' that pops open automatically if cabin altitude ever climbs past 14,000 feet.

name: Protective Breathing Equipment (PBE — Crew Firefighting Smoke Hood)
function: Vacuum-sealed, self-contained aluminized firefighting smoke hood with a neck seal and anti-fog visor. Uses a closed-circuit Potassium Superoxide ($KO_2$) chemical scrubber or compressed oxygen cartridge that absorbs exhaled carbon dioxide and moisture while generating 15 minutes of breathable oxygen for crew fighting an in-flight cabin fire.
location: Cockpit aft wall and Cabin Attendant stations
simple: A silver fire-proof hood stored next to the fire extinguishers in the cabin. If a passenger's laptop battery catches fire in an overhead bin, a flight attendant pulls on this hood so they can walk right into thick smoke with 15 minutes of sealed breathing air.

name: Portable Cabin First-Aid / Walkaround Oxygen Cylinder
function: Portable high-pressure oxygen bottle with shoulder harness, contents gauge, 2 L/min and 4 L/min constant-flow regulator, and disposable oro-nasal mask stowed in cabin brackets for administering medical first-aid oxygen to an unwell passenger or allowing cabin crew to move through the cabin after a depressurization.
location: Cabin overhead stowage bins and attendant wall brackets
simple: Portable green oxygen tanks with shoulder straps stowed in the cabin so flight attendants can give medical oxygen to a passenger feeling faint at cruise altitude without dropping all 180 overhead yellow masks!

name: Bleed Air Monitoring Computer (BMC) / Pneumatic Controller
function: Dual-channel digital pneumatic controller that monitors pressures and temperatures across the engine bleed, APU bleed, and crossbleed ducts. Regulates precooler discharge temperature (~200°C), controls High-Pressure / Intermediate-Pressure bleed transfer, commands the Crossbleed Valve, and monitors twin overheat-detection wire loops for hot bleed-air duct leaks.
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack
simple: The electronic brain of the pneumatic bleed-air system: watches over the 200°C compressed air pipes running from the engines to the wings and air-conditioning packs, shutting the valves down immediately if it detects an overheat or pipe leak.

name: Engine Bleed Pressure Regulating Valve (PRV) & Overpressure Valve (OPV)
function: Pneumatically actuated butterfly regulating and shutoff valve (PRV) that throttles high-pressure engine compressor air down to a steady ~40–45 psi, backed up immediately downstream by a spring-loaded pneumatic Overpressure Valve (OPV) that slams shut automatically if duct pressure ever exceeds ~75–85 psi.
location: Left and Right Engine Pylons / Core Nacelles
simple: Air coming straight out of a jet engine compressor at takeoff power would burst the aircraft's air ducts. The PRV regulates that blast down to a steady 45 PSI, and the OPV sits right behind it as a safety shutoff if pressure ever spikes.

name: High-Pressure Compressor Bleed Valve (HPV) & IP Check Valve
function: Pneumatically regulated butterfly valve tapping the High-Pressure Compressor stage (e.g., 9th stage) paired with a one-way Intermediate-Pressure Check Valve (e.g., 5th stage). At low engine idle (such as descent), the HPV opens to keep manifold pressure up; once the engine spools up for takeoff/cruise, the HPV closes so cooler, more fuel-efficient Intermediate-Pressure air feeds the plane.
location: Left and Right Engine Core High-Pressure Compressor cases
simple: Like an automatic two-speed gearshift for engine air: when the engines are idling slowly during descent, it taps air from the high-pressure back of the compressor; when the engines speed up, it switches to the cooler middle of the compressor to save fuel.

name: Bleed Air Precooler Heat Exchanger & Fan Air Valve (FAV)
function: Air-to-air stainless steel or Inconel crossflow radiator mounted in the engine pylon, cooled by cold engine fan bypass air metered through the butterfly Fan Air Valve (FAV). Cools +350°C to +450°C compressor bleed air down to a regulated +200°C before the duct enters the fuel-filled wing structure.
location: Left and Right Engine Strut Pylons
simple: Air tapped off the engine compressor can reach +400°C—too hot to pipe through an aluminum wing filled with fuel! The Precooler uses a blast of cold air from the big front engine fan (metered by the Fan Air Valve) to cool that bleed air down to 200°C right inside the engine pylon.

name: Pneumatic Crossbleed Isolation Valve
function: Dual-motor electrically actuated butterfly valve (with one motor for AUTO logic and one for cockpit MAN override) bridging the Left and Right pneumatic bleed manifolds. Opens automatically when APU bleed air is supplying both packs/wings, or opens manually for a Crossbleed Engine Start using air from the opposite running engine.
location: Center fuselage belly pneumatic duct bay
simple: Connects the left and right high-pressure air ducts together—allowing the single APU in the tail to feed both wings, or allowing a running Engine #1 to blow compressed air across to start Engine #2.

name: High-Pressure (HP) Pneumatic Ground Air Start Receptacle
function: Standardized 3-inch ISO pneumatic ground coupling with dual non-return check valves mounted behind a lower belly access door. Allows an external diesel Air Start Unit (ASU) cart to pressurize the aircraft's pneumatic manifold (~40 psi) to start the main engines or run the air conditioning packs when the APU is deferred under the MEL.
location: Lower fuselage belly fairing
simple: If the tailcone APU is inoperative, mechanics hook a thick yellow air hose from a ramp compressor truck ('Air Start Unit') into this belly port to blow compressed air into the engines and start them at the gate.

name: Pressurized Potable Water Tank & Water System Air Compressor
function: Filament-wound fiberglass/kevlar fresh-water storage tank(s) (typically 200 to 1,000+ litres) located in the heated under-floor cargo bay. Pressurized to ~25–35 psi by bleed air (or a dedicated oil-free electric air compressor) through a sterilizing filter so clean drinking and hand-washing water flows upwards to all galley boilers and lavatory faucets without individual water pumps.
location: Under-floor pressurized belly bay behind forward or aft cargo hold
simple: Instead of using noisy water pumps for every sink and coffee maker, the aircraft's fresh-water tank is pressurized with compressed air—pushing water smoothly up to every bathroom faucet and galley on the plane.

name: Lavatory Vacuum Toilet Assembly, Flush Valve & Rinse Valve
function: Teflon-coated ultra-low-water toilet bowl fitted with a microprocessor Flush Control Unit (FCU), motorized/pneumatic 2-inch discharge Flush Valve, anti-siphon water Rinse Valve (~200 mL per flush), and Vacuum System Controller. Uses cabin-to-outside differential pressure above 16,000 ft (or the Vacuum Blower below 16,000 ft) to pull waste at 100+ mph into the aft waste tank.
location: Inside each Cabin Lavatory module
simple: Uses less than a cup of water and a 4-second roar of vacuum suction to whisk waste down narrow pipes to the tail tank—powered for free above 16,000 feet by the natural pressure difference between the cabin and the thin outside air!

name: Vacuum Waste Holding Tank, Liquid Separator & Vacuum Blower
function: Aft under-floor composite waste holding tank fitted with ultrasonic/point-level full sensors, a Cyclonic Liquid Separator, and a high-speed 115V 400 Hz AC centrifugal Vacuum Generator Blower. Below 16,000 ft and on the ground, when any passenger presses FLUSH, the Vacuum Blower spins up for ~10 seconds to create the suction needed to evacuate the toilet line.
location: Aft Bulk Cargo / Tailcone boundary
simple: The sealed composite holding tank in the back belly where all toilet waste is stored until the airport lavatory truck drains it at the gate—paired with the electric vacuum motor that creates suction when the plane is on the ground.

name: Air Traffic Services Unit (ATSU / CMU) & GateLink Wireless Router
function: Central data-link router hosting Controller-Pilot Data Link Communications (CPDLC / FANS) for digital ATC clearances and Airline Operational Control (AOC / ACARS) messaging across VHF, HF, and SATCOM links, paired with an airport Wi-Fi/cellular GateLink router for automated flight-ops and maintenance data synchronization.
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack
simple: The digital communications hub that lets pilots exchange text-message clearances directly with Air Traffic Control over oceans (CPDLC) and automatically beams maintenance and operational data to the airline.

name: Fuel Tank Inerting Air Separation Module (ASM) & IGGS Controller
function: Hollow-fiber permeable polymer membrane canister mounted on the Inert Gas Generation System (IGGS / NGS) pallet and managed by a dedicated controller. Filters cooled engine bleed air by allowing fast-diffusing oxygen and water molecules to permeate out overboard while routing dry Nitrogen-Enriched Air (NEA) into the Center Wing Tank so oxygen stays below the 12% flammability limit.
location: Under-wing Belly Fairing Pack Bay
simple: Uses thousands of microscopic hollow polymer straws that let oxygen molecules slip out the sides while trapping pure nitrogen—pumping inert nitrogen gas into the center fuel tank so fuel vapours can never catch fire.

name: Auxiliary Power Unit (APU) Gas Turbine Engine
function: Self-contained constant-speed gas turbine engine mounted inside a titanium firewall enclosure in the unpressurized tailcone. Drives a full-capacity 90–120 kVA 400 Hz AC electrical generator and a dedicated surge-controlled load compressor that supplies pneumatic bleed air for cabin air conditioning on the ground and main engine starting.
location: Unpressurized Aft Tailcone Compartment
simple: The miniature jet engine tucked inside the very tip of the tailcone. It produces zero forward thrust—instead, it makes all the electricity and compressed air the airplane needs while parked at the gate (or as an ETOPS backup in the air).

name: APU Electronic Control Box (ECB / APU FADEC)
function: Full-authority digital electronic controller for the APU mounted inside the pressurized aft cargo bay. Sequences the APU air intake flap, electric starter motor, fuel metering unit, ignition exciter, and bleed/surge load control valves, and triggers an immediate automatic protective shutdown if overspeed, high EGT, low oil pressure, or fire occurs.
location: Aft Bulk Cargo Compartment electronics rack
simple: The digital computer brain for the tailcone APU: manages the entire one-button automatic start sequence, holds speed at a rock-steady 100% RPM, and automatically shuts the APU down if it ever overheats or loses oil pressure.

name: APU Air Intake Flap Actuator & 28V DC Starter Motor
function: Linear electromechanical actuator that swings the flush lower/upper tailcone air intake scoop open when the cockpit APU Master switch is pressed, paired with a high-torque 28V DC battery-powered electric starter motor (or starter-generator) that cranks the APU compressor shaft up to light-off and self-sustaining speed.
location: Aft Tailcone APU compartment
simple: Main jet engines need compressed air from the APU to start—so how does the APU itself start when the whole airplane is dark? This electric actuator opens a hidden air scoop in the tail, and a heavy 28-volt battery motor cranks the APU just like a car starter!

name: Trailing-Edge Static Discharger Wicks & Bonding Jumpers
function: High-resistance carbon-impregnated fiberglass rods with sharp tungsten/wire corona tips bolted along the trailing edges of ailerons, elevators, rudder, and winglets, paired with braided metal Bonding Jumpers across every control-surface hinge. Bleed triboelectric friction static smoothly into the wake without radio noise.
location: Trailing edges of wings, horizontal stabilizer, vertical fin, and winglets
simple: Those thin, pencil-sized rods sticking backward off the edges of the wings and tail. They bleed off the 50,000+ volts of static electricity built up by rubbing against snow and dust in flight so static sparks don't crackle over the pilots' radios.

name: Passenger Cabin Entry / Service Door Assembly
function: Outward-and-forward translating plug or semi-plug passenger cabin door supported on a forged parallel-arm hinge beam. When closed, lifts or settles onto multiple forged steel stop-pads along the fuselage door frame so internal cabin differential pressure (~8.5 psi, or ~10 metric tonnes of total force) wedges the door solidly against the frame.
location: Forward and Aft Left/Right Passenger Entry and Galley Service Doorways
simple: The main boarding and exit doors of the aircraft. When closed, heavy metal stop-pads along the door edges sit behind matching pads on the fuselage frame so 10 tonnes of internal cabin air pressure locks the door shut in flight.

name: Overwing / Mid-Cabin Emergency Exit Door & Automatic Flight Lock
function: Type III or Type I overwing emergency exit hatch/door fitted with an automated 28V DC solenoid Flight Lock Actuator controlled by the landing gear/air-ground logic. Automatically engages a mechanical locking pin across the exit handle as soon as takeoff thrust is applied or speed exceeds 50 knots, and unlocks upon landing rollout.
location: Left and Right Cabin Overwing Exit frames
simple: The emergency exits right over the wings—equipped with an automatic electric deadbolt ('Flight Lock') that clicks shut during the takeoff roll and unlocks on landing so no passenger can tamper with an overwing hatch in flight.

name: Door Damper and Emergency Pneumatic Opening Cylinder
function: Dual-function hydraulic damping strut and high-pressure nitrogen pneumatic actuator linking each passenger door to the fuselage frame. Cushions door swing against wind gusts during normal gate operations (DISARMED); when the door is ARMED and the handle is lifted, fires compressed nitrogen to power-assist the heavy door wide open in 2 seconds.
location: Passenger and Emergency Exit Door hinge support arms
simple: During normal boarding at the gate, this cylinder acts like a smooth hydraulic door closer so wind doesn't slam the heavy door. When the door is set to ARMED, however, lifting the handle triggers a blast of compressed nitrogen inside the cylinder that throws the heavy door wide open automatically!

name: Cabin Door Residual Pressure & Slide Armed Warning Lights
function: Window-mounted LED warning indicator driven by an independent differential pressure switch and girt-bar microswitch. Flashes a red 'CABIN PRESSURE' warning light if engines are off, the slide is disarmed, and trapped cabin pressure exceeds 2.5 hPa (~0.036 psi), or illuminates a white 'SLIDE ARMED' warning light if the handle is moved while armed.
location: Adjacent to the observation window of every cabin entry and service door
simple: Two life-saving warning lights built right into every cabin door window: a white light that warns you 'STOP—the explosive escape slide is still ARMED!' and a flashing red light that warns 'STOP—there is still trapped air pressure inside the cabin!'

name: Forward & Aft Lower-Deck Cargo Doors & Hydraulic Actuators
function: Large outward-and-upward hinged lower-deck cargo doors locked along their lower sill by rotating steel cam latch hooks and locking pins (monitored by proximity sensors for the cockpit DOOR page), and lifted open by twin hydraulic actuators powered by the electric hydraulic pump or ground manual hand pump.
location: Lower right-hand fuselage belly (Forward and Aft Cargo Compartments)
simple: The wide outward-opening cargo hold doors on the lower right side of the aircraft belly, raised and lowered by hydraulic cylinders so baggage containers and pallets can roll inside.

name: Armored Cockpit Door, Electric Lock Strikes & Decompression Latches
function: Ballistic-resistant Kevlar/composite cockpit door secured by redundant electromagnetic lock strikes controlled by a Cockpit Door Locking Control Unit (CDLCU), a pedestal toggle switch (UNLOCK / NORM / LOCK), and an emergency galley keypad. Incorporates pressure-differential blowout panels that release automatically if rapid cockpit decompression occurs.
location: Cockpit aft entrance bulkhead
simple: The bulletproof cockpit door: held locked in flight by electromagnetic bolts controlled by the pilots, while incorporating special pressure-relief panels that pop open automatically if a sudden loss of air pressure ever happens in the cockpit.

name: Composite Nose Radome & Lightning Diverter Strips
function: Hinged aerodynamic nosecone fabricated from quartz or E-glass fiberglass plies sandwiching a hydrophobic Nomex honeycomb core. Engineered to be transparent to 9.3 GHz X-band weather radar beams while resisting hail/bird impact, and fitted with exterior segmented metallic Lightning Diverter Strips that guide lightning strikes safely back to the metal airframe.
location: Extreme forward nose tip ahead of the forward pressure bulkhead
simple: The hinged fiberglass nosecone of the airplane. Because radar waves can't pass through metal, the nosecone is built from fiberglass honeycomb that lets the weather radar see storms 300 miles ahead—lined with thin metal lightning strips on the outside.

name: Forward & Aft Pressure Bulkheads
function: Curved dome or stiffened flat structural walls (aluminum alloy or carbon-fiber composite) that seal the front and rear ends of the pressurized fuselage cabin tube (ahead of the nose radome and ahead of the unpressurized tailcone), carrying the full axial membrane tension load of 8.5 psi cabin pressurization across 30,000+ flight cycles.
location: Forward nose (Frame 1) and Aft cabin boundary ahead of tailcone
simple: The pressurized passenger cabin is shaped like a giant soda can: these two curved structural walls are the front cap and back cap that hold the pressurized air inside the cabin while leaving the nosecone and tailcone unpressurized.

name: Fuselage Frames, Longitudinal Stringers & Under-Wing Keel Beam
function: Semi-monocoque primary fuselage skeleton: hoop-shaped Circumferential Frames (maintaining cross-sectional shape and stopping crack propagation with tear straps), longitudinal Stringers/Longerons (carrying fuselage bending loads), and the massive reinforced ventral Keel Beam that bridges bending loads past the unbolted Main Landing Gear wheel-well cutout.
location: Full length of fuselage shell and lower wheel-well centerline
simple: The internal skeleton behind the cabin walls: circular rib hoops ('Frames') keep the tube round, lengthwise rails ('Stringers') stop the fuselage from sagging, and a massive backbone girder ('Keel Beam') carries loads past the big hole cut in the belly for the landing gear.

name: Engine Strut Pylon Box, Mounts & Fuse Pins
function: High-strength titanium and steel primary torque box cantilevered ahead of the wing leading edge, wrapped in heat-resistant Aft/Rear Pylon Fairings (APF/RPF). Suspends the turbofan engine via Forward and Aft Engine Mounts and calibrated Fuse Pins engineered to transmit thrust, weight, and gyroscopic loads while cleanly shearing away if an extreme gear-up ground impact occurs so the wing fuel tank isn't torn open.
location: Between Left/Right Wing Front Spar and Engine Nacelle
simple: The rugged titanium and steel support strut that hangs a 4-tonne jet engine underneath the wing—connected with calibrated 'Fuse Pins' designed to break away cleanly in a severe wheels-up slide so the engine doesn't rip open the wing fuel tank.

name: Horizontal Stabilizer Box & Left/Right Elevator Surfaces
function: Carbon-fiber composite (CFRP) and aluminum Trimmable Horizontal Stabilizer (THS) tailplane pivoting on rear-spar trunnion bearings and driven at its front spar by the THS jackscrew, with hinged Left and Right honeycomb Elevator surfaces attached to the rear spar for primary pitch control.
location: Aft Empennage Horizontal Tailplane
simple: The horizontal tail wings and hinged elevator flaps at the back of the aircraft that generate downward aerodynamic force to balance the nose and pitch the plane up and down.

name: Vertical Stabilizer Fin Torque Box & Rudder Surface
function: Carbon-fiber composite (CFRP) Vertical Stabilizer fin box anchored to heavy fuselage tailcone frames via six triple-lug shear/tension fittings, supporting the single-piece composite honeycomb Rudder hinged along its rear spar and embedded with exterior copper mesh for lightning protection.
location: Aft Empennage Vertical Tailfin
simple: The giant vertical tailfin and hinged rudder that give the airplane directional weathervane stability and counter asymmetric thrust if one engine fails.

name: Cockpit Laminated Windshields & Sliding Direct-Vision Windows
function: Six-panel flight deck glazing assembly: Left and Right Front Windshields built from three chemically strengthened glass plies laminated with thick Polyvinyl Butyral (PVB) energy-absorbing interlayers and 200V AC anti-ice heating film (rated to stop a 4-lb bird strike at 350 knots); Left and Right Sliding Side Windows on crank tracks for ground ventilation or emergency rope escape; and Fixed Aft Side Windows.
location: Cockpit forward window frame
simple: Inch-thick, three-layer armored glass windshields heated by an invisible electric film to survive 350-knot bird strikes—flanked by two middle side windows that pilots can physically unlock and crank open on the ground.

name: Passenger Cabin Triple-Pane Acrylic Window & Breather Hole
function: Stretched cast acrylic (PMMA) window assembly sealed into the fuselage window forging: a thick Outer Pane carrying 100% of normal cabin pressurization load, an unloaded fail-safe Middle Pane pierced by a tiny bottom 'Breather / Bleed Hole' (equalizing inter-pane pressure and preventing fogging), and a thin scratch-guard Inner Plastic Reveal attached to the cabin sidewall.
location: Left and Right Passenger Cabin fuselage sides
simple: Two structural panes of high-strength stretched acrylic plus an inner scratch cover. The tiny hole at the bottom of the middle pane lets cabin pressure push solely against the outer pane—keeping the middle pane completely unstressed as a 100% backup!

name: Wing Front/Rear Spars, Ribs, Gear Support Rib & Jacking Dome
function: Primary load-bearing wing box structure formed by the Front Spar, Rear Spar, milled Upper Skin (compression load, 7075 aluminum or CFRP), Lower Skin (tension load, 2024 damage-tolerant aluminum or CFRP), internal Chordwise Ribs (which double as sealed integral fuel tank baffles), heavy forged Gear Support Rib, and under-wing Tripod Jacking Socket.
location: Center Wing Box (through lower fuselage) and Left/Right Wings
simple: The hollow structural beam box inside each wing that carries the entire weight of the aircraft in flight—while its sealed internal compartments double as the aircraft's main fuel tanks!

name: Wingtip Sharklet / Blended Winglet Device
function: 2.4-meter-tall aerodynamically sculpted carbon-fiber composite wingtip extension bolted to the outboard wing tip rib. Diffuses spanwise airflow and blocks high-pressure under-wing air from curling over the tip into a strong vortex, increasing effective aspect ratio and cutting Lift-Induced Drag by 3% to 5%.
location: Outboard Left and Right Wingtips
simple: The tall, gracefully curved upright winglets ('Sharklets') at the tips of the wings that weaken swirling wingtip air tornadoes and save hundreds of tonnes of jet fuel every year.

name: Wing Leading-Edge Slats & Curved Steel Roller Tracks
function: Segmented aluminum leading-edge high-lift airfoils (e.g., Slats 1 to 5 per wing) mounted on forged steel curved circular-arc tracks that roll on needle bearings through sealed cans in the front wing spar. Extending slats opens a converging aerodynamic slot that re-energizes the upper wing boundary layer and raises the critical stall angle by ~8–10 degrees.
location: Left and Right Wing Leading Edges
simple: Curved metal panels along the front edge of each wing that slide forward and down on curved steel roller tracks during takeoff and landing—opening a slot that keeps airflow hugging the wing at steep climb and approach angles.

name: Inboard & Outboard Fowler Flaps, Track Beams & Canoe Fairings
function: Single- or double-slotted Fowler trailing-edge flap panels supported on four forged steel/titanium Flap Track Beams and multi-roller Carriages under each wing (streamlined inside composite canoe-shaped Flap Track Fairings). Slide rearward first to increase wing surface area, then tilt downward to increase camber for low-speed takeoff lift and steep landing drag.
location: Left and Right Wing Trailing Edges
simple: The massive panels at the back edge of the wings that roll backward and tilt down along steel beams hidden inside those canoe-shaped pods under the wing—making the wing both bigger and more curved for slow-speed takeoffs and landings.

name: Upper-Wing Spoiler Panels & Outboard Aileron Surfaces
function: Carbon-fiber honeycomb control surfaces hinged to the wing rear spar: five or six upper-surface Spoiler panels per wing (serving triple duty as asymmetric Roll Spoilers, symmetric in-flight Speedbrakes, and full-deflection Ground Lift-Dumpers on touchdown) plus outboard Aileron panels that droop ~5° when flaps extend to boost wing lift.
location: Wing Trailing Edge upper and outboard positions
simple: The flat carbon-fiber doors on top of each wing (Spoilers) that pop up to help bank the plane, slow down in flight, or dump all wing lift on touchdown, plus the outboard Ailerons.

name: Engine Acoustic Air Intake Cowl & Gull-Wing Fan Cowls
function: Aerodynamic forward Inlet Cowl lined with perforated acoustic honeycomb panels (tuned to absorb fan blade-passage noise and fitted with an anti-iced D-duct nose lip) followed by hinged Left and Right composite Fan Cowl doors with telescopic hold-open struts and 3/4-bellmouth bottom latches that enclose the external engine accessories.
location: Forward section of Left and Right Engine Nacelles
simple: The streamlined front intake ring (lined with thousands of tiny sound-deadening pinholes) plus the two big hinged side doors that mechanics prop open on steel struts to service the outside of the engine.

name: Engine Nacelle Ecological Drain Collector & Pylon Drain Mast
function: Multi-tube manifold and streamlined drain mast projecting from the bottom of the engine fan cowl (6 o'clock position). Separately channels any trace seal weepage from the IDG, hydraulic pump, fuel metering unit, starter, and oil tank into individual labeled drain ports so a line mechanic can identify which accessory seal is leaking by checking which tube is dripping.
location: Bottom center (6 o'clock) of each Engine Fan Cowl
simple: A streamlined fin at the very bottom of the engine cowling containing several separate little drain pipes—each connected to a different pump seal so mechanics can tell at a glance whether a drip is fuel, hydraulic Skydrol, or engine oil!

name: Turbofan Front Fan Blades, Fan Disk (LLP) & Kevlar Containment Case
function: Wide-chord titanium or 3D-woven carbon-fiber front Fan Blades dovetailed into a forged titanium Fan Disk (Life-Limited Part) coupled to the Low-Pressure Booster stages on the N1 shaft. Surrounded by an armored Kevlar/metallic Fan Containment Case engineered to catch and contain a broken fan blade at 100% takeoff RPM without penetrating the cabin.
location: Front section of Left and Right Turbofan Engines
simple: The giant spinning front fan that produces up to 80% of a modern jet engine's thrust by pushing a massive wall of cold bypass air around the outside of the engine core—wrapped inside a bulletproof Kevlar belt.

name: High-Pressure Compressor (HPC) Rotor/Stator & Annular Combustor
function: Multi-stage axial compressor (N2 core spool) with titanium/nickel-alloy rotor disks (LLPs) and Variable Stator Vanes that squeeze incoming air up to 35–50:1 pressure ratio and +600°C before it enters the Annular Combustion Chamber—where 12 to 28 fuel nozzles atomize Jet A-1 into a continuous +1,700°C flame suspended inside a film of cooling air.
location: Central core module of Left and Right Turbofan Engines
simple: The heart of the jet engine: 8 to 14 rows of spinning blades squeeze air to 40 times atmospheric pressure, mix it with a mist of jet fuel, and burn it continuously inside a ring-shaped furnace.

name: High-Pressure Turbine (HPT) & Low-Pressure Turbine (LPT) Modules
function: Single-crystal nickel-superalloy High-Pressure Turbine blades (grown from a single metallic crystal, coated with ceramic Thermal Barrier Coating, and perforated with laser-drilled film-cooling holes so they survive gas temperatures 300°C above their own melting point!) driving the N2 compressor, followed by multi-stage Low-Pressure Turbine (LPT) rotors driving the big N1 front fan.
location: Hot aft core section of Left and Right Turbofan Engines
simple: Single-crystal superalloy turbine blades sitting right behind the combustion fire that extract tens of thousands of horsepower from the roaring exhaust blast to spin the front fan and compressor.

name: Engine Accessory Gearbox (AGB) & Radial Drive Shaft
function: Curved aluminum/magnesium gear casing mounted on the bottom of the fan case or core, mechanically driven off the High-Pressure (N2) compressor shaft via an internal bevel Transfer Gearbox and hollow Radial Drive Shaft. Provides splined mounting pads for the IDG electrical generator, Engine-Driven Hydraulic Pump, Fuel Pump/HMU, Oil Pump, Air Turbine Starter, and Permanent Magnet Alternator (PMA).
location: Lower fan case or lower core of Left and Right Engines
simple: A mechanical gearbox slung under the engine and spun by a vertical shaft from the engine's N2 core—providing the mounting pads that spin the fuel pump, oil pump, hydraulic pump, electrical generator, and starter.

name: Electronic Engine Control (EEC / FADEC) & Data Storage / Rating Plug
function: Dual-channel (Channel A and Channel B) Full Authority Digital Engine Control computer shock-mounted on the cold fan case and powered independently above ~12% N2 by its own gearbox-driven Permanent Magnet Alternator (PMA), paired with a plug-in Data Storage Unit / Thrust Rating Plug. Controls all fuel scheduling, auto-starting, variable airflow valves, and N1/N2 overspeed limits.
location: Engine Fan Case exterior
simple: The dual-channel supercomputer bolted right onto the side of the engine fan case (FADEC). Powered by its own dedicated mini-generator on the gearbox so it keeps running even if the aircraft loses all electrical power, while a small plug-in memory chip sets the engine's certified thrust rating.

name: Hydro-Mechanical Unit (HMU) / Fuel Metering Unit (FMU) & HP Fuel Pump
function: Gearbox-driven two-stage High-Pressure Fuel Pump (centrifugal LP stage + positive-displacement gear HP stage, plus a replaceable fuel filter) integrated with an electro-hydraulic Fuel Metering Unit (FMU / HMU). Translates electrical torque-motor commands from the EEC into precise metered fuel flow to the combustor nozzles AND high-pressure 'servo fuel' used as hydraulic muscle to move engine air valves.
location: Engine Accessory Gearbox
simple: The mechanical muscle obeying the FADEC computer's brain: pressurizes jet fuel up to 1,000+ PSI, filters it, meters the exact amount of fuel into the combustion fire, and even uses high-pressure fuel as 'hydraulic fluid' to move the engine's internal air valves!

name: Engine Interface Unit (EIU)
function: Dedicated airframe-to-engine concentrator LRU (one independent box per engine: EIU 1 and EIU 2) mounted in the forward avionics bay. Interfaces cockpit engine panels, ADIRU air data, FMGC autothrust commands, and bleed-air pack demands with the wing-mounted EEC (FADEC), and routes 115V AC aircraft power to the EEC before the engine's own alternator comes online.
location: Forward Avionics Bay rack
simple: The dedicated translator box in the nose avionics bay (one strictly for Engine 1, one strictly for Engine 2) that connects the aircraft's cockpit switches and air-conditioning computers to the FADEC computer out on the wing.

name: High-Energy Ignition Exciter Box & Dual Igniter Plugs (System A & B)
function: Two independent capacitor-discharge Ignition Exciter boxes (System A and System B) mounted on the engine fan case that step 115V AC power up to ~15,000–20,000 volts stored in high-energy capacitors, firing intense 1-to-4-joule plasma sparks across two recessed surface-gap Igniter Plugs protruding into the combustion chamber.
location: Engine Fan Case (Exciter Boxes) and Combustor Casing (Igniter Plugs)
simple: Unlike a car spark plug that fires weak little sparks continuously, a jet engine igniter stores 20,000 volts in a capacitor and fires blinding, loud plasma lightning snaps (1 to 2 times per second) to light freezing Jet A-1 mist during starting or heavy rainstorms.

name: Variable Stator Vane (VSV) & Variable Bleed Valve (VBV) Actuators
function: Fuel-pressure-powered ('servo-fuel') linear actuators controlled by the EEC via the HMU that rotate the unison rings of the High-Pressure Compressor Variable Stator Vanes (VSVs) and modulate the Booster Variable Bleed Valves (VBVs). Prevent destructive compressor stall and surge during rapid throttle slam accelerations/decelerations.
location: Engine High-Pressure Compressor Casing
simple: Pivots entire rows of stationary air-guide vanes inside the compressor as engine speed changes—making sure the compressor never chokes or 'backfires' (compressor surge) when the pilots slam the throttles forward or back.

name: HPT / LPT Active Clearance Control (ACC) Cooling Valve & Manifolds
function: EEC-controlled butterfly valve that meters cool fan bypass air into perforated spray manifolds wrapped around the outside of the High-Pressure and Low-Pressure Turbine casings during cruise. Gently cools and shrinks the outer metal turbine ring by fractions of a millimeter around the spinning blade tips—eliminating tip-leakage gaps to boost EGT margin and cut cruise fuel burn.
location: Wrapped around the exterior of the Engine Turbine Casing
simple: Once the engine settles into cruise at 36,000 feet, this valve blows cool fan air onto the outside of the hot turbine case—shrinking the metal case slightly so it hugs the spinning turbine blade tips tighter and stops wasted gas from leaking past the tips!

name: Throttle Control Unit (TCU — Thrust Levers) & Engine Master Switches
function: Center pedestal Engine 1 and Engine 2 Thrust Levers coupled to a mechanical artificial-feel detent box (REV FULL, IDLE, CL, FLX/MCT, TOGA) and dual-channel RVDT rotary angle resolvers (TCU) wired directly to the EEC, paired with the two guarded ENG MASTER 1 & 2 switches and rotary ENG MODE selector (CRANK / NORM / IGN-START).
location: Cockpit Center Pedestal Throttle Quadrant
simple: The cockpit thrust levers and Engine Master switches. Moving a thrust lever into the 'CLIMB' or 'TOGA' click-detents spins precision angle sensors under the console that send the pilot's thrust request straight to the engine computers.

name: Exhaust Gas Temperature (EGT) Thermocouple Harness & N1/N2 Speed Sensors
function: Array of 8 to 12 Chromel-Alumel (Type K) thermocouple probes arranged in a ring around the Low-Pressure Turbine inlet/outlet (wired in parallel to average gas-path temperature for the cockpit EGT gauge and EEC redline monitoring), plus magnetic-reluctance N1 Fan speed and N2 Core speed pickup probes.
location: Engine Turbine Case (EGT Probes) and Fan/Gearbox Case (N1/N2 Sensors)
simple: A ring of heat-resistant temperature probes sitting right in the 900°C turbine exhaust stream plus magnetic speed counters on both shafts—feeding the primary engine gauges (N1, EGT, N2) on the upper cockpit display.

name: Engine Vibration & Health Monitoring Unit (EVMU / PHMU) & Accelerometers
function: Piezo-electric vibration accelerometers mounted on the #1 bearing frame and turbine frame feeding a dedicated Engine Vibration / Prognostics Health Management Unit (EVMU / PHMU). Uses tracked-filter Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) processing to separate N1 fan vibration from N2 core vibration on the cockpit display, and computes optical fan-blade trim-balance weights for mechanics.
location: Engine Fan Case or Forward Avionics Bay
simple: A digital stethoscope for the engines: separates front-fan vibration from core-shaft vibration on the cockpit screen so pilots spot bird-strike blade damage immediately—and tells mechanics on the ground exactly which fan bolt needs a heavier balance weight.

name: Thrust Reverser Translating Cowls / Blocker Doors & Hydraulic Control Unit (HCU)
function: Electro-hydraulic Thrust Reverser Hydraulic Control Unit (HCU — incorporating an isolation valve, directional valve, and independent third-line-of-defense mechanical/electric Tertiary Lock) that pressurizes four hydraulic actuators per engine on touchdown. Slides the aft translating cowl rearward (or deploys 4 pivoting blocker doors) to block the cold bypass duct and redirect fan air 45° forward through cascade vanes.
location: Aft Fan Cowl / Bypass Duct of Left and Right Engines
simple: When the wheels touch down and pilots pull up the reverse levers, the HCU unlocks three independent safety locks and slides the back half of the engine cowling rearward—swinging internal blocker doors shut so the front fan blasts air forward to slow the plane down.

name: Engine Oil Tank, Lubrication & Scavenge Pump, FCOC & Magnetic Chip Detectors
function: Closed-loop dry-sump synthetic turbine oil system: pressurized Oil Tank with sight glass and remote transmitter, gear-driven Supply & multi-element Scavenge Pump unit, Fuel-Cooled Oil Cooler (FCOC — transferring bearing heat into incoming engine fuel so the oil cools and the fuel warms above freezing!), Scavenge Oil Filter with differential pop-out indicator, and Magnetic Chip Detectors (MCDs) in each bearing return line.
location: Engine Fan Case / Accessory Gearbox
simple: Circulates synthetic oil through the 15,000-RPM engine bearings, uses incoming cold jet fuel to cool the hot oil inside a heat exchanger (warming the fuel so it can't ice up!), and traps any microscopic steel bearing flakes on magnetic plugs.

name: Pneumatic Air Turbine Starter (ATS) & Starter Air Shutoff Valve (SAV)
function: High-torque axial air turbine motor with planetary reduction gearing, sprag overrunning clutch, and magnetic oil plug mounted on the engine accessory gearbox, fed by an electrically/manually controlled butterfly Starter Air Valve (SAV). Uses ~40 psi APU or ground-cart compressed air to accelerate the N2 core shaft during engine start, then automatically decouples via its sprag clutch at ~50% N2.
location: Left and Right Engine Accessory Gearboxes
simple: A compact, screamingly powerful air turbine bolted to the engine gearbox. At pushback, compressed air from the tailcone APU blasts through this starter to crank the heavy engine core up to starting speed before fuel is lit, then uncouples automatically once the engine runs on its own.
